item.title: Former US Marine Robert Gilman released from detention in Russia
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 2.58
Former US Marine Robert Gilman released after years of detention in Russia Gilman's release came amid concerns about his health. Robert Gilman, a U.S. citizen and former Marine, has been freed from years of detention in Russia on humanitarian grounds, a State Department spokesperson confirmed Tuesday. "Thanks to the hard work of President Trump and Special Envoy Witkoff, Mr. Gilman joins over 100 Americans whom the United States has freed during President Trump's second term in office. This Administration will continue to work for the release of all Americans unjustly detained in Russia, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard," the spokesperson said. Gilman's release came amid severe concerns about his health. According to the organization advocating on behalf of his family, Gilman is on his way to a U.S. military hospital in Texas, where he will be medically and psychologically assessed and treated. His family has flown to Texas, including his mother, who was in Russia attempting to see him at the hospital. Gilman, now 32 years old, had been detained since 2022. Later that year, he was sentenced to four and a half years in a prison colony after being accused of fighting with a Russian police officer at a train station. Gilman's family deny the charges and have accused the Russian authorities of wrongfully detaining him for political purposes because he is American. According to the "Free Robert Gilman" website, Gilman served in the U.S. Marine Corps and also founded "Robert Gilman Just English" to help students in Poland build their English skills. Gilman was in Moldova to teach and was visiting family outside of Moscow when he fell ill and was then accused of kicking a police officer. Gilman, who was recently designated as a wrongful detainee, was not part of a prisoner exchange, and no other concessions were provided as part of his release, according to the State Department spokesperson. President Donald Trump said he had discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin about Gilman's release, adding that "Russia asked for no one in return -- No exchange took place." "Robert will land at Andrews Air Force Base, in Washington, D.C., tonight, where my Representatives, some of whom are on the plane with him, will welcome Robert back to THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA! I just spoke to him, and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands," Trump wrote in a post on his social media account Tuesday. Lexie Hudson, Gilman's sister, commented on his release in a press release sent by Global Reach, a nonprofit organization dedicated to bringing home Americans who are wrongly held abroad. Hudson thanked both Trump and Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Ed Markey. "The Russians treated my brother so badly," Hudson said. "They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both an American and a Marine. What did they get out of this? Why did they do this to such a wonderful person?" "I am looking forward to seeing Robert. I haven't been able to speak with him once since this all began. We will make sure that he gets the treatment and support that he needs." Sen. Markey celebrated Gilman's release in a post on X while also describing Gilman's debilitating condition. "Approximately 50 days ago, Robert was diagnosed with a dissociative stupor -- a condition where he is non-responsive and unable to interact or eat. He was essentially catatonic and also suffered a severe case of pneumonia. We don't yet know the full details of his current condition or the long-term impact on his recovery. I'm grateful that Robert is now on his way back to the United States to receive the life-saving care that he desperately needs," Markey wrote. Gilman's family members and representatives have said that in addition to the false charges levied against him, Gilman was subjected to torture and harsh physical and mental abuse by Russian prison guards. Moscow has so far not commented on Gilman's release.

item.title: Retired firefighter suffered brain injury after eating oysters at steakhouse: Lawsuit
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 2.47
Veteran, retired firefighter suffered brain injury after eating oysters at Illinois steakhouse: Lawsuit He remains hospitalized over a year since the catastrophic health complications. CICERO, Ill. -- An Illinois man who served as a Marine and firefighter remains hospitalized more than a year after suffering catastrophic health complications that his attorneys allege were caused by contaminated raw oysters eaten at a steakhouse. Attorneys representing Joe Belgio announced a lawsuit and fundraiser on his behalf, alleging he suffered permanent brain injuries after becoming ill following a meal at Gibsons Steakhouse in Oak Brook. Family, friends and community members gathered in support of Belgio, whose fiancé, Melanie Stayer, said the couple had been celebrating with family at the restaurant in June of last year. Their daughter was 5 months old at the time. "He's one of the rarest people you will ever meet in your life. He was a God-fearing man. Success to him was having a family," Stayer said. According to the lawsuit, Belgio became severely ill after eating raw oysters, leading to a medical crisis that ultimately resulted in permanent injuries. "I want people to be aware that this could happen to anyone. This was a casual day with a casual man at a restaurant that he wanted to celebrate life with his family, and life can change so quickly," Stayer said. Belgio, once described by loved ones as a strong and healthy man, is now confined to a hospital bed, according to his attorneys. Attorney Scott O'Sullivan said Belgio's condition deteriorated rapidly. "He ended up getting very, very ill, and resulting in cardiac arrests where he lost consciousness and oxygen for at least eight minutes, and was revived by this very fire department, and has been in the hospital ever since," O'Sullivan said. The lawsuit alleges doctors screened Belgio for bacteria and identified several pathogens that attorneys say are associated with shellfish contamination. O'Sullivan said the injuries have left Belgio with severe, long-term impairments. "He is most likely bedridden for the rest of his life. He is extremely brain damaged, with very little cognitive capacity, and will need care for the rest of his life," O'Sullivan said. A spokesperson for Gibsons Oak Brook disputed the allegations, saying in a statement: "There have been no other reported cases of illness. Based on the facts and our internal investigation, there is no evidence to suggest that our establishment caused his health condition. We are confident that a fair and thorough legal process will agree with this conclusion." The lawsuit also names Supreme Lobster and Seafood Company as a defendant. The company had not responded to a request for comment. Stayer said the man she knew for his service to others has been permanently changed by the ordeal. "This is a man who deployed. He ran into burning buildings, and you thought he was out of the line of fire, and really, he wasn't," she said. As the lawsuit moves forward, members of Belgio's former fire department are working to help ease the burden of his ongoing recovery and care, while supporters continue fundraising efforts for his family.

item.title: El-Sayed spoke with Obama as Michigan Democrats look to unite
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 2.08
El-Sayed spoke with Obama as Michigan Democrats look to unite El-Sayed says he hopes the former president will campaign with him. BRIDGEWATER, N.J. -- BRIDGEWATER, N.J. (AP) — Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, said Sunday he has spoken with Barack Obama and hopes the former president campaigns with him as the party tries to unite after a bitter primary that exposed deep rifts between its progressive and moderate wings. El-Sayed said his Friday conversation with Obama was “really warm and inspiring." The candidate did not provide details. “I was grateful for his advice. It was very warm, very inviting, and I know that he knows the critical role that Michigan is going to play,” El-Sayed told NBC’s “Meet the Press." Asked if he would like to see Obama come to Michigan to drum up support for Democrats before the midterm elections in November, El-Sayed said he “really” hoped so and that Obama “knows a lot about winning Michigan” after carrying the state in the 2008 and 2012 presidential races. An Obama spokesperson confirmed the call. The discussion came the same day that a group of Michigan nominees and other notable national Democrats tried to present a united front at a rally in Detroit. The crowd cheered loudest for El-Sayed, a former public health official who last week narrowly beat establishment-backed U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in a contentious and closely watched primary. A Democratic victory in the fall is crucial to the party's chances of regaining a Senate majority. Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is not seeking reelection in the perennial swing state, which Republican Donald Trump won in 2016 and 2024, while Democrat Joe Biden carried in 2020. El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman who narrowly lost the Senate race to Democrat Elissa Slotkin in 2024 and has tried to capitalize on lingering tensions within the Democratic Party. Rogers has released a video message attempting to appeal to Democrats who feel their party may be moving too far to the left with El-Sayed. “You have a home with us," Rogers says in the video. During an interview Sunday with CNN's “State of the Union,” El-Sayed acknowledged that "we aired our differences” in the heated primary. But he said the internal divisions are "so much smaller than the similarities that we share.” “You’re seeing folks come together,” El-Sayed said, before adding of moderate Democrats, “We might see the world differently. But we also recognize the responsibility to come together.”

item.title: New train service connects Finland and Sweden for first time in decades
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 5.62
- Published A new passenger train linking Finland and Sweden has begun running, creating the first rail connection between northern Finland and southern Europe in nearly 40 years. Shortly after 05:00 local time (03:00 BST) on Monday, a double-decker train set off from the coastal Finnish city of Oulu, rumbling its way across the border to Sweden. As the inaugural service crossed the Torne river from Finland and pulled into Sweden's Haparanda station, it was met by crowds of people waving Finnish and Swedish flags. The route was initially suspended in the late 1980s to the early 1990s, due to low passenger numbers and technical differences in the tracks between Finland and Europe. Finland uses the same track widths as Russia, which are wider than the European standard - a holdover from when the Nordic nation was part of the Russian Grand Duchy in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is currently in the process of updating its track widths to match the European standard. The new, twice-daily journey to Sweden's Haparanda takes 100-minutes as it hugs the west coast of Finland before crossing the border between the two Nordic neighbours. Passengers travelling on from Haparanda will need to transfer onto a different train to continue southward. But the service makes it possible to travel around 5,000km by rail from Portugal's Algarve to Finland's northernmost train station of Kolari - believed to be the longest train route in Europe. It will also enable a 24-hour train journey between capitals Helsinki and Stockholm. Finland's transport minister said the return of the cross-border service shows cooperation between the two countries was growing "all the time". Elisa Markula, chief executive of Finland's state-owned railway operator VR, said she hopes the service will benefit from a "renaissance" in rail travel across Europe. "Train travelling in all Europe is having a renaissance. Also in Finland, our passenger numbers are increasing a lot," Markula told AFP.

item.title: Thailand suspends new gun permits after mass shooting
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.42
- Published Thailand's government will immediately stop issuing gun permits after a shooting incident last week in which a 14-year-old killed eight people and himself. Existing gun owners are already banned from carrying their weapons in public. The South East Asian country has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in the region, with around 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, and high levels of gun crime. In response to the recent shooting, the prime minister has promised to pass tough new gun control laws with severe penalties, suspending new permits in the meantime. Last Friday, a pupil at Debsirin Nonthaburi School outside Bangkok shot his grandparents using a handgun owned by his grandfather, before opening fire at teachers and students at school, authorities say. Both grandparents, five staff members at the school and one 12-year-old girl died. They say there is evidence that the boy watched violent content online, and that he showed a strong interest in learning how to handle guns. His consumption of this content as well as anxiety over studies and family issues might have also fuelled his actions, they add. Until further notice, no new permits to purchase or own guns will be issued. Existing purchase permits will not be renewed but it is unclear what will happen to existing gun ownership permits. Permits to carry guns were suspended in late 2023 - owners must keep their weapons at home or at a shooting range. The government is also considering measures to persuade the owners of an estimated four million unlicensed guns to hand them over in the wake of the school shooting. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has said the announced measures will remain in place as the government works to pass new gun control laws, with stronger controls and significantly harsher penalties. Gun control advocates have called for mental health assessments as part of the permit process, and for permits to be periodically re-evaluated. Anutin has said stricter ammunition controls are in his sights, while the education minister has proposed screening at the entrance of schools to stop students from bringing in weapons.

item.title: Houthis reportedly kill four in first deadly attack since start of Iran war
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.36
- Published Six people have been killed and 10 injured in strikes by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on a cargo ship in the Red Sea, the internationally recognised government of Yemen has said. The transport ministry said the vessel was hit with three ballistic missiles, south of the port of Mocha, causing a fire on board and resulting in the deaths of four crew - three Pakistanis and one Indonesian. Yemen's coastguard later said a second deadly missile strike targeted rescuers who tried to evacuate the ship. The Houthis said they hit a ship carrying Saudi military equipment. It appears to be the first deadly attack by the group on a vessel since the US and Israel began striking Iran on 28 February. The Houthis launched their attacks on shipping last month - announcing a naval blockade of Saudi ports. The conflict in the region has been ongoing for more than five months, punctuated by a faltering ceasefire which was meant to lead to a deal to end the war. It has whipped up regional tensions, with the Houthis also attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and oil facilities, in parallel with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway where a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit. The latest attack comes after a years-long truce in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government collapsed last month. The Houthis control much of north-western Yemen, and frequently clash with the government. The government operates out of Aden in the south, due to the capital Sanaa being held by the Houthis. Social media images examined by BBC Verify appear to show a damaged cargo ship in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which sits at the inlet of the Red Sea, off the coast of Yemen. In its statement, the Yemeni government said the ship had been carrying food, and that the attack on a commercial vessel marked an escalation in approach from the Houthis. In an earlier statement, maritime risk management company Vanguard said the Yemeni Navy deployed to assist the vessel and came under fire. This resulted in three others being injured. Close-up pictures show the vessel is named Tihamah which, according to ship-tracking platform MarineTraffic, is in the Red Sea off Warner Point. Vanguard has identified the ship as sailing under the flag of Tanzania, while shipping website MarineTraffic says it is owned by an Egyptian operator. In its statement, Yemen's ministry of transport referred to Tihama as a "Yemeni commercial ship", while earlier reports in Iranian media referred to it as "Saudi-affiliated". The pictures of the vessel, which were shared by Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency, have been verified as new and show no signs of AI-generation. Additional reporting by Ghoncheh Habibiazad

item.title: Libyan authorities battle big blaze at major oil refinery
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.00
- Published Libyan emergency services have been battling to contain a huge blaze at a major oil plant after it was targeted by unknown attackers. The Zawiya refinery, west of the capital Tripoli, was hit in a drone strike on Monday evening - the third such incident in two days. The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said a tank containing about 4.5m litres of fuel was directly hit, triggering a huge fire that caused it to collapse. It said it was considering suspending operations if the attacks continued. There were no "serious injuries" from the fire, with most patients treated for smoke inhalation, Libya's Ambulance and Emergency Service said on Tuesday. The Zawiya refinery is the largest operational facility in Libya, with an output of 120,000 barrels per day. The NOC condemned similar attacks in past days in Zawiya, including two drone strikes on a naphtha reservoir and a water desalination plant. It called on the authorities to investigate who was behind the violence. The attacks have highlighted continuing instability in Libya, which has been split in two since a civil war broke out after the ousting of former leader Muammar Gaddafi. Colonel Gaddafi seized power in 1969 and ruled autocratically for four decades until he was toppled and killed in 2011 in a rebellion assisted by Western military intervention Since his fall, rival power centres, one based in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, and one in the west in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, have been jostling for political and military dominance.

item.title: Luigi Mangione appears in court as questions remain in case ahead of murder trial
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.97
- Published The jury in the New York state trial of Luigi Mangione will remain anonymous, the judge overseeing the case ruled on Tuesday. Mangione has pleaded not guilty to the killing of UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson outside a Manhattan hotel in December 2024. The case has been at the centre of an online frenzy between Mangione's backers - many of whom see the 28-year-old as a symbol of the backlash against US healthcare costs - and his critics, who analyse his intentions and possible political views. In Tuesday's hearing, Judge Gregory Carro decided the 12-person jury would be anonymous to the public because of the intense spotlight on the case. Mangione attended the final pre-trial hearing dressed in a charcoal grey suit with his hair clipped short. He sat silently at the defence table while his attorneys conferred with the judge. The trial begins next month, with jury selection scheduled to start on 8 September. Mangione, if found guilty, could face decades behind bars. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including second-degree murder and weapons-related offences. He faces a separate federal trial next year, in which he has also pleaded not guilty. Here's what to know about the upcoming trial, and what questions remain. Who will be able to watch? Mangione's lawyers and prosecutors have traded terse court filings debating how much access the public will have to the trial. The public are allowed to watch court proceedings in New York, but seating space is often limited for high-profile cases. Mangione's trial is expected to generate significant media interest from both traditional journalists as well as streamers and social media influencers. Mangione's supporters have demanded more transparency, and frequently post and broadcast from outside court. On Tuesday, Carro said the court would open an overflow room, which will allow more people to attend. Caro pushed back against prosecutors for raising security concerns about an overflow room, telling them it was not the court's "first rodeo" with blockbuster cases. The judge also rebuked Mangione's attorneys for their filings, saying any suggestion the district attorney's office was involved in the process "is simply incorrect". What evidence will be seen by the jury? One of the most crucial elements of the Mangione case was decided in a multi-day hearing in December, where the judge weighed which evidence prosecutors could present during trial. Mangione's team wanted to exclude evidence recovered from his Pennsylvania arrest. It alleged that state police improperly seized and searched Mangione's possessions, and did not properly advise him of his constitutional rights before questioning him. The defence succeeded in excluding some items, including a gun magazine, cell phone, passport, wallet and computer chip found in Mangione's backpack. But Judge Gregory Carro allowed at trial a gun and notebook with Mangione's purported writings, viewed as vital to the prosecution. Prosecutors have unveiled surveillance footage showing the moment Thompson was shot from behind by a hooded individual. They also used footage to piece together Mangione's alleged movements after the shooting, and ballistics and fingerprint evidence they claim bolsters their case. What might Mangione's defence look like? Mangione's legal team has yet to unveil its full strategy. So far, his lawyers have not offered a robust alternative theory to the one prosecutors have put forth. "We do not have, like in 'The Fugitive,' the idea of the one-armed man who's the real killer," said former federal prosecutor Mitchell Epner, referencing the 1993 Harrison Ford thriller about a man wrongly convicted of killing his wife. Earlier this summer, Mangione's lawyers proposed, then quickly withdrew, an "extreme emotional disturbance" argument. In such a defence, New York law requires lawyers to show a defendant "acted under the influence of extreme emotional disturbance for which there was a reasonable explanation or excuse". Extreme emotional disturbance would allow the jury to consider the less severe charge of manslaughter, rather than second-degree murder. But jurors would have to be convinced of the accused's state of mind at the time. Mangione's team did not immediately respond to a request for comment. As in every US criminal trial, the burden rests on the prosecution to prove its case to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt, a high legal bar. "The more his case is about the question of who killed the victim, the easier it is for the prosecution," said Epner. Epner cited other themes, including healthcare in America, as potential narrative threads that could sway a jury in Mangione's favour. "The more it's about the other peripheral issues, the harder it is for the prosecution," he said.

item.title: The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.62
- Published The WNBA is still in the midst of its 2026 season and yet it is next year's Draft for North America's top women's basketball league that is dominating the headlines. Why? Because some former men's NBA players have declared they will enter for selection - citing the current eligibility guidelines, or lack of, for transgender women players. "I'm officially declaring myself a WNBA prospect," said Enes Kanter Freedom, who played 11 seasons in the NBA. It is the latest development in a story ignited by a comment made by Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham, who said she wanted to protect young girls "who shouldn't have to go against biological men" in sport. Her words have instigated protests - albeit not grand in scale - on both sides of the argument, and once again catapulted the debate around transgender women in sport into the spotlight. How did we get here? Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the topic of "protecting" women's sports. The Indiana Fever guard said she had received criticism from people who believed she "hated" transgender people, something she denied. She said she wanted to "extend love" to everyone, but added: "I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men." She later doubled down on her comments, saying it was "common sense", external to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports. Her words quickly moved beyond basketball and into a wider political debate in the United States. President Donald Trump expressed his support for Cunningham, while vice-president JD Vance said she was "inspiring". Though the 29-year-old later said she is "not a very political person", her remarks have followed her around the country. Competing rallies from critics and supporters were organised at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests. The scale of the debate in the media, online and in politics was striking given no openly transgender woman is due to play, or has ever played, in the WNBA. What do the rules say? The WNBA operates under a collective bargaining agreement (CBA), a deal negotiated between the league and its players association (WNBPA), setting rules on matters including player salary caps, revenue sharing, benefits and overall league operations. On player eligibility, the CBA states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." The WNBA has yet to comment publicly on the row since Cunningham's comments but league commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week in which she said the matter would be discussed at an upcoming pre-arranged meeting with team presidents. In the memo, seen by the Associated Press, external, Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league". She added: "Our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities." However, the lack of detail in the league's eligibility criteria has been brought to light by Kanter Freedom, who finished his playing career with the Boston Celtics in 2022. "If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," he wrote on Instagram, external. Kanter Freedom, who has previously spoken out about human rights violations in China and Turkey, among other issues, added: "I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices. "I'm simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone - the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for." A day after Kanter Freedom's 'announcement', Royce White - who made three appearances in the NBA as a player and is now a Republican Senate candidate - said he would also declare for the Draft, adding: "I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball." Whether the vagueness of the rules are by design to leave it open to transgender women or a sign of an oversight that genuinely needs tightening up is not clear. BBC Sport has contacted Cunningham's representatives, the WNBA and WNBPA for comment. What has the reaction been? Cunningham's comments have become a flashpoint inside a league which has a long history of player activism on issues including race, gender equality and LGBTQ+ rights. The players' association did not mention Cunningham by name when it eventually addressed the debate. In a statement the WNBPA denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" and reaffirmed its commitment to "justice, equity, diversity and inclusion". It called on fans to report abusive behaviour at games and added that it would continue to have "hard" conversations but it "will not be used as political pawns". There is strong feeling on both sides of the argument. Minnesota Lynx head coach and president Cheryl Reeve, who said: "I come from a space of inclusion. "The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports." Reeve wore a "Trans Kids Belong" T-shirt before Minnesota played Indiana earlier this month and was seen speaking to Cunningham on court before the game. Cunningham later said the pair had exchanged their perspectives and that the conversation ended with "love and respect". Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams said she would welcome a transgender athlete "on my team or against my team, any time". Last month, the WNBA suspended Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton from attending the team's next five home games after an exchange with two fans, who were sat courtside displaying signs thanking Cunningham for "speaking up for girls". Keaton reportedly confronted the teenage fans and admonished them during the game. The Storm have since apologised. As for Cunningham, the attention has increasingly become an unwelcome distraction. Having defended her original comments, she said recently that she now wanted the conversation to return to what was happening on court. "I want to get back to basketball, it's always been about basketball" she said, arguing that the standard of play in the WNBA was being overshadowed by issues away from the game. But that may prove difficult, as pressure grows on the league to clarify exactly who is eligible to play. What are the rules in other sports? In recent years, many governing bodies in sport have amended their rules about the inclusion of transgender athletes at the elite level, moving more towards restrictions. Athletics, cycling and aquatics, for example, have implemented outright bans on transgender women taking part in women's events. In March, it was announced that the women's category of Olympic sports will be limited to biological females from the LA Olympic Games in 2028. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) says eligibility will be determined by a "once-in-a-lifetime" sex test, which would prevent transgender women and those with differences in sexual development (DSD) who have gone through male puberty from competing. In the United States, transgender women and girls are banned from competing in women's sports categories in schools, universities and the grassroots level. That was part of an executive order - titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" - signed by President Trump last year. It does not cover professional sport.

item.title: Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.53
- Published Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country in the Middle East to formally end capital punishment. A majority of MPs in the 128-seat parliament backed the measure on Tuesday, while Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voted against it. The legislation will now go to the cabinet before being passed to President Joseph Aoun for signing. The government has already expressed its support for the measure. Lebanon has not carried out an execution since January 2004, although courts have continued to hand down death sentences. Rights groups estimate that more than 78 people remain on death row. Under the new legislation, capital punishment will be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour. However, the legislation does not yet set out in detail how the new sentence would be enforced. Hard labour is already written into Lebanese law but has rarely been implemented in recent years. The country's financial crisis and overcrowded prisons have limited the authorities' resources and capacity. The latest legislation follows years of campaigning by civil society groups and lawyers for the removal of capital punishment from Lebanese law. "We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," Oragit Younan told the BBC. As co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights, she led a nearly three-decade campaign to abolish the death penalty in Lebanon. "We are in a war, and people [have been] killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win. We can be a model for others," she said. Tuesday's vote in parliament follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions. An execution required a decree signed by the president, prime minister and justice minister - but no such decree has been signed since 2004. Under Lebanese law, the death penalty could previously be imposed for some of the country's most serious offences, including aggravated murder, certain terrorism-related crimes resulting in death, treason, espionage and offences against state security. Previous attempts to abolish the death penalty have failed, including legislation introduced in parliament in 2004 and a proposal from the justice ministry in 2008. Lebanon's move comes as the use of the death penalty remains contested elsewhere in the Middle East. Jordan resumed executions in June, carrying out its first since 2017. In Israel, its parliament has approved legislation that allows for the expansion of the circumstances in which capital punishment can be imposed. Israeli MPs passed a new law in May to impose the death penalty and conduct public trials for those involved in the Hamas-led attacks and mass hostage-taking in Israel in October 2023. Elsewhere, the UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear among the population and suppress dissent". In Iran, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests, UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said earlier this month.

item.title: France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.50
- Published France has banned unsolicited telemarketing phone calls, in what a consumer group is hailing as a "small revolution" for the sales industry. From Tuesday, unsolicited calls are prohibited for businesses in all sectors - but there are some exceptions. Calls will only be permitted if they relate to a contract a person has already entered into or the company has obtained prior consent to be contacted for marketing. "It cannot be stressed enough that peace and quiet is a right, and it is time to stop exposing consumers to unwanted solicitations," consumer advocacy group Que Choisir Ensemble, said in a statement. "This observation also holds true online and on the street, which are saturated with demands to consume," group president Marie-Amandine StÃ©venin added. She said the group had long been advocating "for an end to the automatic assumption that someone in their home or private life is a potential customer." "This is a victory for consumers, the vast majority of whom do not want to receive sales calls," she said. But the law change has riled some business groups, and officials in Morocco, where the call centre sector is heavily reliant on the French market. One government minister estimated the telemarketing restrictions could lead to the loss of up to 50,000 jobs, according to a report in Moroccan newspaper Le Matin. The head of France's direct-selling trade association, the FÃ©dÃ©ration de la Vente Directe (FVD), also criticised the reforms for adding what he said were administrative burdens for businesses. "You'll have to obtain written consent from your customer, and you'll also have to keep proof of that consent," FrÃ©dÃ©ric Billon said in comments reported by the New York Times. According to a 2025 parliamentary report, 97% of people are annoyed by telemarketing calls, with the authors wryly noting it is "one of those rare issues that unites people in France". The same report found 72% of French people reported being contacted on their mobile phones at least once a week, while 38% said they were called once a day. Germany, Austria and Italy are among the European countries that impose significant restrictions on telemarketing calls, often referred to as cold calls. In the UK, most telemarketing calls are legal provided the recipient has not objected to the call and their number is not on a statutory list of people or businesses who do not want to receive calls.

item.title: Watch: What we know about Tupac murder suspect Duane 'Keffe D' Davis
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.37
Watch: What we know about Tupac murder suspect Duane 'Keffe D' Davis The only suspect ever charged for the drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 is Duane "Keffe D" Davis. The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He has pleaded not guilty. The BBC's journalist Anoushka Mutanda-Dougherty explains what we know about the suspect. Read more about the case here.

item.title: Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.26
- Published Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles. Ukraine said strikes on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia - which killed seven people and injured at least 24 - involved ballistic missiles from Russia's ally. In Voronezh, western Russia, warehouses of the biggest online retailer Wildberries were hit by Ukraine. The company, known as Russia's Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks. The attacks come a day after at least 13 people were killed, including one child, in Ukrainian drone strikes on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, more than 1,100 km (680 miles) from the Ukrainian border. In a video address on Monday evening, Zelensky said "for the first time" Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea". "The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots", Zelensky said, adding that this poses a danger to the rest of the world. He has not presented any evidence to back up his comments. It is not the first time Zelensky as well as other senior Ukrainian and Western officials have accused Russia of receiving military assistance from North Korea. Ukraine's military has said that says dozens of North Korean missiles have been fired by Russia into its territory since Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The Ukrainian president warned over the weekend that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight with Russian forces. Some 11,000 North Korean soldiers were deployed to help Moscow push Ukrainian troops out of the western Russian region of Kursk following their cross-border incursion in August 2024. In January 2025, Western officials told the BBC that North Korean troops had suffered nearly 40% casualties in the fighting there in just three months. In his Monday's address, Zelensky also hailed a successful air strike on a Russian petrochemical plant in western Siberia on Monday as a "very significant achievement" by the Ukrainian military. He promised "more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary". Zaporizhzhia regional head Ivan Fedorov posted photos of vehicles and buildings on fire, saying Moscow had struck the city using missiles and guided bombs. All seven casualties were employees of Ukraine's Zaporizhstal metallurgical plant, which later halted all its operations. One person was injured in strikes on the capital Kyiv, where air raid sirens sounded twice during the night. Explosions could be heard on the outskirts of the capital, triggering fires. Local officials later said a children's hospital was damaged - but there were no injuries as staff and patients were sheltering. Two women have been injured in a Russian drone strike on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Sumy, according to regional head Serhii Kryvosheienko. He later said that one person was killed when Russia attacked the city with gliding bombs in the afternoon. Meanwhile, strikes on substations in Kherson and Kharkiv resulted in power outages. Ukrainian officials say Russia fired 120 drones overnight and a range of different missiles, but for the first time they have not given a number of missiles fired or intercepted. It follows an Air Force statement on Monday urging the media not to write "sensationalised headlines" or "spread pessimism" about the shortage of air defence interceptors. Separately, there have been reports of a fire and explosions at a logistics centre of Wildberries in the Voronezh region. Wildberries has not yet confirmed the attack, but said that its facilities in the region, which borders Ukraine, have been evacuated. In July, Ukrainian drone attacks on several retail warehouses belonging to Wildberries disrupted the operations of a large number of small and medium-sized Russian businesses. Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army. The attack on Tatarstan this week was one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. At least 75 people were injured in the strikes, with Ukraine's Armed Forces saying it had hit the city's Tanevo oil refinery. Verified images on social media showed large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background. The Uzbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan.

item.title: Watch: Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.19
Watch: Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river Workers waded through a rubbish-filled river in Manila, collecting waste that washed in during days of heavy rain. The nine-day downpour, exacerbated by tropical storms, was equivalent to more than a month's worth of rain in some areas. It resulted in school and government office closures across the main island of Luzon and flooding in the capital. Floods, landslides and accidents driven by the rains killed at least 16 people in the northern Philippines, rescuers said on Monday

item.title: Russia releases former US Marine reported in poor health
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.13
- Published President Donald Trump said a former US Marine held in a Russian prison, whose health was reportedly in extremely poor condition, has been released. "After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that no prisoner swap took place. Robert Gilman, who is from Massachusetts, was arrested in 2022 for allegedly kicking a police officer while aboard a train. He had recently been moved from prison to a civilian hospital in Russia after going into a catatonic-like state. Gilman was on a flight back to the US accompanied by his mother, doctors, and members of the administration. The BBC understands Gilman is expected to arrive early on Wednesday morning at a US military hospital in Texas where he will be assessed and treated. Trump said he spoke to Gilman on the phone, "and he had one request â A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!" "During my Administration, we have prioritised bringing home Americans detained abroad, and have done so at a level never seen before," Trump added. Gilman's health was in "life-threatening condition" after he was subjected to "harsh and abusive treatment", his family said in a statement. "The Russians treated my brother so badly. They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both and American and a Marine," his sister, Lexi Hudson, said. "I am so grateful to President Trump for saving my brother's life," she added. Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey also helped secure her brother's release, she said. In a statement, Markey said: "Approximately 50 days ago, Robert was diagnosed with a dissociative stupor - a condition where he is non-responsive and unable to interact or eat. " Kieran Ramsey, chief investigative officer for Global Reach, the advocacy group representing the former Marine, told Reuters that Gilman was released because the Russian government realised "they're not losing any geopolitical power position by releasing him. This is a humanitarian release". Gilman served in the US Marines for a year until August 2020. He was arrested for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk aboard a train to Moscow in January 2022 and was initially given a sentence of three and a half years. He was later found guilty of assaulting prison guards, after he allegedly attacked a prison inspector during a cell check. His sentence was increased to 10 years. In Russian confinement, Gilman was subjected to repeated harassment, including forced exercise training sessions that lasted up to 16 hours and the administration of psychotropic drugs, Eric Lebson of Global Reach told CBS, the BBC's US media partner. The abuse was so severe that at one point Gilman had required a feeding tube in his nose, according to Lebson. He said five other Americans remain in Russia, each contending with medical issues. Their names are Aleksandr Antonov, David Barnes, Olga Jezler, Andre Khachatoorian and Chuck Zimmerman. "While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X. "The President will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home," he continued.

item.title: Watch: Family escapes home during Colombia earthquake
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.26
Watch: Family escapes home during Colombia earthquake A family captured video of the moment they fled their home during an earthquake in Colombia. Liliana PÃ©rez Ocampo and her family escaped moments before their home was rocked by a 7.4 magnitude quake on Monday. "At first, we thought it was just a mild tremor like the ones that usually happen in Colombia, but when more than 30 seconds passed and everything was shaking harder, we realised it was an earthquake," the mother-of-five told the BBC World Service. Her family, including two young children at school, are safe. "In the end, material things can be replaced," she said. "The most important thing is life, and we have that." With at least 169 people killed, this has been the strongest earthquake to hit Colombia in the 21st Century, according to the country's Geological Service.

item.title: Vietnam's VinSpace taps SpaceX for first satellite launches
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 6.03
Vietnam's only private space company on Tuesday signed a deal with SpaceX to launch its first satellites into orbit next year. The satellites will fly aboard a 2027 mission under SpaceX's Transporter rideshare program, which allows multiple customers to share the same rocket and split satellite launch costs. What do we know about VinSpace and SpaceX? The company, VinSpace, said it would develop and operate the satellites itself, using the missions to test technology in orbit and pave the way for future commercial services. "Reliable access to space is fundamental to turning satellite innovation into operational missions," VinSpace CEO Thu Vu said. The company did not disclose how many satellites it plans to launch, their specifications or the value of the contract with Elon Musk's SpaceX. What is VinSpace? VinSpace was established in November 2025 by Vingroup, Vietnam's largest privately-owned conglomerate. The group was founded by Pham Nhat Vuong, Vietnam's richest man. It has interests ranging from real estate, retail and tourism to healthcare and education. In recent years, Vingroup has increasingly expanded into technology, including electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, robotics and aerospace. VinSpace says it ultimately wants to become a full-service aerospace company, with capabilities spanning satellite design and manufacturing, launch management, satellite operations and space-based data services. What are Vietnam's ambitions in space? Vietnam has been building its space capabilities for decades but remains a relatively small player in the global industry. It launched its first telecommunications satellite in 2008 and a second in 2012. The government has set a goal of becoming a mid-level space power in Southeast Asia by 2030, with satellite technology seen as part of a wider drive to develop high-tech industries. In March, Vietnam opened a major space science and technology center at Hanoi's Hoa Lac High-Tech Park, aimed at expanding domestic satellite development and the use of space-based data. In April, Vietnam licensed SpaceX's Starlink for its first large-scale trial of satellite internet, which uses thousands of low-Earth-orbit satellites to provide high-speed connectivity. item.title: Bulgaria drone crash a wake-up call for country's defenses
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.42
When a drone entered Bulgaria's airspace on Saturday and exploded in a sunflower field near the northeastern village of Kardam — about 100 meters (328 feet) from a border checkpoint with Romania — the immediate question was where the aircraft had come from. Following an on-site check, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was a Ukrainian-manufactured Maya decoy aircraft used to activate and deceive enemy drone systems. And while both Bulgarian and Ukrainian officials confirmed that the first drone explosion on Bulgarian territory since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was in no way deliberate, the case quickly became politically charged. The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador on Monday and stressed that "any unauthorized entry into Bulgarian airspace is unacceptable." Kyiv promised to cooperate fully in clarifying the circumstances of the incident. What is known about the incident? At 8:10 a.m. local time on Saturday, a blast was heard by a police patrol near the Kardam checkpoint on the border between Bulgaria and Romania. Police and military units cordoned off the area once the exact location of the fallen drone was established in a field. In his first statement on the matter, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said there had been neither casualties nor damage to infrastructure but claimed that the drone had been carrying a "significant amount of explosives." Officials on the ground painted a less dramatic picture, saying the explosion did not even create a crater and that only a few sunflowers had been damaged. Drone came down near gas pipeline The drone crashed about a kilometer (0.6 miles) from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine, and in close proximity to a Romanian station. This initially raised questions about whether this key infrastructure could have been a potential target. Prime Minister Radev said that neither Romanian, Bulgarian nor other NATO radars had detected the drone, pointing to the country's lack of advanced equipment capable of detecting traces of such small aircraft, which usually fly very low. Wake-up call for Bulgaria Saturday's drone incident was a wake-up call for Bulgaria in terms of its defense capability. "Yes, we need new [anti-drone] systems that need to be bought fast," Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Monday in an interview with public broadcaster BNT. While Bulgaria recently reinforced its aerial defense capacity in the northeastern part of the country following an increase in the number of drone incursions in neighboring Romania, these defenses did not prevent the airspace breach. Stoyanov said Bulgaria wants to acquire up to 10 anti-drone and electronic warfare systems through the EU's SAFE mechanism and speed up radar purchases, though he admitted this would still be insufficient to provide "comprehensive coverage" of the country. "Drone wars have been waged next to us since 2023, and no concrete measures have been adopted," he said, adding that Bulgaria does not currently have an anti-drone strategy but that his ministry will prepare one. With NATO members scaling up their aerial defenses, Bulgaria now joins the list of countries in Europe that have registered drone incursions linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Was Russia involved? As the decoy drone was partially destroyed, officials have yet to establish its exact trajectory before it crossed Romania and entered Bulgaria. According to Stoyanov, the drone's GPS system was not protected, which could have allowed its movement to be manipulated. Although he did not actually name Russia as potentially being behind the incident, he said the crash could have been caused by what is known as a spoofing campaign, an electronic attack that manipulates a drone's GPS signals. He also pointed to a possible technical failure, as the aircraft's chip was found to be defective. The Defense Ministry declined to say whether the hypothesis of Russian spoofing was being actively investigated and referred DW's questions to the Military Prosecutor's Office, which had not replied by the time of publication. Russia praises Bulgaria's 'restrained' response Former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, however, feels that it is most likely that Russia played a role in the drone crash. "The most probable hypothesis is that electronic warfare led to the loss of control over this drone as a result of Russia's actions," Tagarev told DW, adding that Bulgarian authorities have the necessary information to rule out this possibility if it is not the case. As the investigation continues, the government has not publicly mentioned Russia and is instead seeking answers from Ukraine. The handling of the case was even welcomed in Moscow, with Yuri Pilipson, a senior representative of the Russian Foreign Ministry, praising Radev's government for its "more restrained" and "more rational" rhetoric toward the war in Ukraine. Crash highlights Bulgaria's 'more pragmatic' foreign policy shift The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry used the incident to reiterate that security in the region can only be achieved through diplomacy after it summoned the Ukrainian ambassador. "This war will not be decided on the battlefield, but through diplomatic steps," said Defense Minister Stoyanov, echoing the prime minister's longstanding position. A former president and fighter jet pilot, Radev won an absolute majority in parliament in April with his Progressive Bulgaria party. While the country had until then steadfastly supported Ukraine, the new government brought a change in the country's foreign policy, promising a "more pragmatic" approach, including toward the war in Ukraine. Over the past three months, Bulgaria has halted state arms supplies to Ukraine, blocked the EU's efforts to include the head of the Russian Orthodox Church in its sanctions package and declined an invitation by French President Emmanuel Macron to join the Coalition of the Willing, which brings together more than 30 countries supporting Ukraine. "I think the Bulgarian foreign minister was too quick to summon the Ukrainian ambassador rather than the Russian one," Tagarev told DW. "It doesn't matter whose drone it is, but rather whose actions caused it to end up here." Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

item.title: Colombia earthquake: Rescuers race to find thousands missing
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.81
Rescuers and volunteers searched through collapsed buildings across western Colombia on Tuesday after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake caused widespread destruction across several major cities a day prior. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said at least 181 people died in the quake, while around 2,595 people were injured. While the president said around 195 people are missing, civilian-run databases indicate at least 3,900 people are still unaccounted for. What do we know about the western Colombia earthquake? The quake struck near the community of San Jose del Palmar in the western region of Choco on Monday, causing widespread destruction in the cities of Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo and Buenaventura. Cali accounted for 85 deaths and Pereira 66, according to the association. The figures remain incomplete because they largely cover major cities and do not yet include the full toll from rural communities. Thousands have been reporting missing, with many feared trapped beneath collapsed buildings. Around 1,600 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. Soldiers, emergency teams and relatives have been clearing debris in dozens of towns and cities, with volunteers forming lines to pass chunks of concrete by hand. The cities of Pereira, Cali, Quibdo and Manizales remain on red alert because of the scale of the damage. At least 165 buildings completely collapsed in those cities alone. Hospitals, airports, public utilities and transport systems have also been damaged across several western departments. The epicenter was near one of Colombia's poorest and most isolated regions. Large parts of the area can be reached only by boat, aircraft or through jungle routes, while damaged roads and other infrastructure are complicating access. That means the full extent of casualties and destruction near the epicenter remains unclear. How has the world responded? The United States has offered $15.5 million (€13.42 million) in emergency assistance, while the European Union has activated its Copernicus satellite service to support rescue operations. The EU has also begun providing emergency assistance following the earthquake, including €100,000 in initial aid through the German Red Cross. Israel, Mexico, Chile, Argentina and El Salvador have also offered assistance. The earthquake was felt beyond Colombia, including in parts of Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama. Why was such a deep quake so damaging? The scale of the destruction was striking because the earthquake struck at a depth of around 100 kilometers (62 miles), where surface shaking would normally be expected to be weaker. Geologist Raul Perez of Spain's Geological and Mining Institute told EFE news agency that the magnitude 7.4 quake was a particularly complex subduction event involving the Nazca and South American tectonic plates. He said a "site effect" in some areas amplified the seismic waves as they passed through local geological formations, increasing both the strength and duration of the shaking and worsening damage to buildings. Perez said the combination of the quake's unusual depth, its magnitude and the local amplification effects made it an event that would need to be studied closely. Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier Don't let the algorithm hide the news.
