item.title: Middle East: Trump took secret flight out of Turkey over Iran threat
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.48
What you need to know This blog is now closed. Below are developments in the war in Iran and wider conflict in the Middle East from Tuesday, August 11: - Trump confirmed he took a secret flight out of Ankara after July's NATO summit, amid threat from Iran, after the Washington Post first reported it - US-Iran talks on peace and reopening Strait of Hormuz hit impasse - Israel and Venezuela resume consular ties after 17-year break - Lebanon abolishes death penalty in regional first - Oil prices steady after massive gains as market loses hope for a deal Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. Trump confirms secret flight but downplays threat US President Donald Trump told reporters that he secretly switched aircraft after a NATO summit in Turkey last month following security advice from the Secret Service and military over a potential threat. "Well, it's only up to Secret Service. I just follow what they'd like to do, so I go by Secret Service and the military," Trump said. An initial report by the Washington Post on Monday said Trump was moved from Air Force One to a smaller military aircraft via an airport catering vehicle, while aides and journalists remained on the presidential plane. Trump confirmed the switch but said he was not concerned by any threat. "I guess there was a threat out there. I didn't really ask too much about it. I get a lot of threats," Trump said. "I have a lot of threats that you don't know about. Any consequential president has a lot of threats. Non-consequential presidents don't get threats." US says forces fired on tanker in Gulf of Oman US Central Command on Tuesday said its forces fired on a Panama-flagged tanker in the Gulf of Oman Tuesday after the vessel's crew ignored warnings to stop. CENTCOM said the crew of a Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two hellfire missiles into the engine room of the M/V Vela Nova, disabling its steering. The ship was said to be in violation of a US blockade of Iranian ports when attacked by the US chopper. A CENTCOM post on X said the Vela Nova is "no longer transiting to Iran." The statement went on to say that the US had redirected 55 commercial ships in violation of the blockade, adding that it had disabled three non-compliant vessels and boarded two more. The US Navy currently has more than 15 warships deployed to the Arabian Sea, including two aircraft carriers and an amphibious assault ship. Lebanon becomes first Middle East country to abolish death penalty Lebanon's parliament voted to abolish capital punishment on Tuesday, making it the first country in the Middle East to do away with the death penalty. The country has not carried out an execution since 2004, but until Monday had continued to hand out death sentences. In January, the rights group Amnesty International (AI) said that at least 85 individuals were in death row cells in Lebanon. To date, death sentences have handed down for crimes such as murder, terrorism or espionage, which will now be punished with life sentences involving hard labor. Justice Minister Adel Nassar, who attended Tuesday's parliamentary session, called the vote a "historic step" for Lebanon. The European Union said Lebanon was "setting a powerful example for other countries in the Middle East and beyond," whereas UN rights chief Volker Türk called on Lebanon's neighbors "to follow its lead in ending this inhumane practice." UN Special Coordinator for Lebanon Jean Arnault said the change "advances the country's adherence to international human rights standards and justice with human dignity." Capital punishment is commonly meted out across the region, with Amnesty International documenting more than 2,000 executions in Iran last year and more than 350 in Saudi Arabia. Israel, Venezuela renew consular ties after 17 years Israel and Venezuela on Tuesday announced the resumption of consular ties after a diplomatic break of 17 years. "Following talks held in recent weeks and days between Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and Venezuelan Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia, Israel and Venezuela have agreed to renew consular relations," read a statement from Israel's Foreign Ministry. "The talks resulted in an agreement to establish a coordination mechanism that will enable the provision of consular services to citizens of both countries." Venezuela, along with Bolivia, broke off diplomatic relations with Israel in 2009 over an Israeli offensive in the Gaza Strip. Tuesday's announcement comes in the wake of generous Israeli disaster relief for Venezuelan earthquake victims. It also comes as new Venezuelan leader Delcy Rodriguez's administration adopts a markedly more cooperative stance towards US President Donald Trump after he ordered the abduction and arrest of her predecessor, Nicolas Maduro. A joint statement said both Israel and Venezuela recognize "the importance of the relationship between the State of Israel and the Jewish community residing in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, which serves as an important bridge of historic friendship between the two countries." Syria sentences Assad to death in absentia A Syrian court has sentenced former President Bashar Assad to death in absentia. Assad was ousted in December 2024 after rebel forces swept into Damascus, ending more than five decades of rule by the Assad family. He and his family to Russia, where he was granted asylum. Moscow is understood to have refused to extradite the toppled dictator. For more on the story, you can check out our article here. Container ship reportedly hit by missile in Gulf of Oman A container ship is believed to have been struck by a missile in the Gulf of Oman, according to maritime security sources. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said it had received a report of an incident involving a commercial vessel and military forces, later correcting the vessel type from a tanker to a container ship. Initial assessments identified the vessel as the Panama-flagged Vela Nova. British maritime risk management group Vanguard and a separate maritime security source said the ship was believed to have been hit while sailing around 71 nautical miles (132 kilometers) off Pakistan's coast. Three killed in reported Houthi attack on cargo ship Three crew members have been killed in a reported Houthi attack on a commercial vessel near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, according to Yemeni government-linked sources. Two Yemeni coast guard sources and two military officials said the Iran-aligned group attacked a deck cargo ship on Tuesday. Yemeni pro-government broadcaster Al Yumhuriya said the vessel was hit by a missile and that the dead were two Pakistani nationals and one Indonesian. The ship's name and nationality were not immediately given. Yemeni government sources said authorities were working to confirm the circumstances of the attack. US has 'swept entire Strait of Hormuz' of mines: Trump President Donald Trump said that the US has cleared the Strait of Hormuz of mines, and that the critical trade route was open to commercial traffic. Trump told reporters at the White House that the US had 100% control of the waterway. "A little bit complex because they [Iran] will, on occasion, drop a mine, and we find the mines. You know, we've mine swept the entire Strait," he said. Trump's comments came as Washington and Tehran have been negotiating the full reopening of the strait for some time. Iran has linked the route's reopening to concessions from the US and its allies while affirming plans to charge commercial vessels passing through the strait. Trump responded to the concessions demand saying he too would demand compensation from Iran, for all the people injured or killed in the conflict. Over the last weekend, US Vice President JD Vance said that Iran had laid a large number of mines in the Strait at he beginning of the war. READ: Is Iran's middle class being pushed into poverty? The war has intensified Iran's economic crisis, squeezing household budgets, hurting businesses. Read DW's report on growing fears that millions of middle-income families in Iran are slipping closer to poverty. Oil prices steady after increase, as hopes for a deal fade Global crude oil prices steadied on Tuesday, after a significant rise amid persisting uncertainty over the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude and US crude futures were both up slightly on Tuesday morning, reaching the highest levels since July 31, after the contracts spiked roughly 5% on Monday. The price of Brent hovered just under $88 (€76) a barrel, having swing between $72 and $102 last month. Oil prices have risen around 10% over the past week, fanning inflationary fears and revitalizing expectations of a possible US interest rate hike in 2026. "We're now in a bit of a Mexican standoff, if you'd like, in terms of who blinks first," Tony Sycamore, a market Analyst at IG told Reuters. "This is going to be almost a war of attrition now," he said. "You probably can see the (oil) market sitting around the $75 to $95 range while we wait to see who blinks first." Trump took secret flight out of Turkey over Iran threat — report US President Donald Trump reportedly departed from Turkey on a secret military flight in July, instead of flying aboard an older Air Force One plane as announced by the White House. This was in response to a credible Iranian assassination threat, the Washington Post reported, as the monthslong war continued. Trump had taken the newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit in July. However, he unexpectedly announced he would used an older Air Force One when departing the country, "for old times's sake." The move had then raised questions over the donated jet's safety. Trump boarded the older Air Force One in front of cameras but was secretly shuttled by an airport catering truck to a smaller plane, an Air Force C-32A, the Washington Post said, citing corroborating material and a US official familiar with the operation. Journalists aboard the decoy Air Force One, where they believed they were to be accompanied by the US President, said they had been advised to keep their window shades closed in the press cabin. When they inquired about it later, Trump said it was because they were "probably on a dangerous flight." "But if I go, you go. Right?" he added. The White House did not directly address the report. Communications director Steven Cheung told the Post there were "many enemies of America" targeting Trump and that every available tool was being used to counter threats. Welcome to our coverage Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of the war in Iran and developments from across the Middle East. US President Donald Trump reportedly took a secret flight out of Turkey after the NATO summit in July, according to the Washington Post. The report describes how the US President was smuggled into a smaller plane, provoking mental visuals straight out of a Hollywood movie, to thwart a possible assassination attempt by Iran. Trump meanwhile, has scoffed at Iran's demands of concessions and reparations, saying he too would seek conflict compensations as part of a peace deal. With this, negotiations over a truce and the possible reopening of the Strait of Hormuz seem to have hit a wall once more. The news had an effect on global markets as well, initially sending oil prices soaring, but they have now stabilized. Stay tuned!

item.title: Key issues in Zambia's 2026 general election
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.44
Zambia's general election on Thursday will be fought on economic recovery, governance reforms and a sweeping change to the country's parliamentary map. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, leader of the United Party for National Development (UPND), is seeking a second term against 14 opponents. His principal challenger is Brian Mundubile, a former ally of the late President Edgar Lungu, who has surged to the front of a fragmented opposition after being backed by a coalition of rival parties. The Electoral Commission announced in April that 70 new constituencies would be added, raising the number of parliamentary seats from 156 to 226, creating smaller, more local voting districts. Up to 8.7 million voters are expected to take part in the elections, a majority of whom are women. Economic issues dominate election campaign Economic issues dominate voters' concerns. Official data shows that over 70% of the population lives on less than three dollars a day, and many households survive on salaries between $60 and $100 (€52 and €87) a month while grocery prices keep rising. "I would like the new government to increase our salaries. [Maize meal] is very expensive. Everything is expensive," said security guard Lucky Mutelo. Rebecca, a market shopper, echoes the sentiment, noting that "the cost of living is still too high." The government has been making significant gains on these issues. Hichilema's government has secured a landmark debt restructuring agreement, restoring an International Monetary Fund program and supporting economic growth. Inflation fell to 6.5% in June this year. The administration has also rolled out free education and an expanded Constituency Development Fund, which allocates public money directly to each of the country's constituencies to finance community-driven local development projects and infrastructure. Nevertheless, a historic drought that crippled agriculture and forced severe hydro‑power load‑shedding has strained household finances. Election demographics amid a fragmented electoral field To become president, a candidate must secure 50% plus one of the total votes cast. If no contender reaches this threshold, the two highest‑scoring candidates will face off in a second round — a mechanism designed to ensure that the president enjoys a clear popular mandate. There are 14 names on the ballot, so even small swings in support across the ten provinces could determine whether the election goes to a second round. Analysts say the election's outcome would hinge on urban centers such as Lusaka and the Copperbelt, where cost‑of‑living pressures are most acute, while rural provinces traditionally follow established party loyalties. Rural voters in the Southern, Western and North‑Western provinces historically back the UPND, whereas the opposition targets the Northern, Luapula and Eastern provinces. Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported that the high youth turnout that propelled the current president Hakainde Hichilema to a landslide victory in 2021 is expected to be a decisive factor again, especially in the densely populated urban districts. Nearly half of registered voters are aged between 18 and 35, making young people a potentially pivotal bloc, Institute for Security Studies researcher Zenge Simakoloyi told AFP. Can women swing this election? Gender representation is another prominent theme. In this election, there is one female candidate for president, and four female running mates. Mwaka Nyirenda is one of a handful of women contesting for a parliamentary seat. "Politics is still a man's world. People doubt you, underestimate you and try to intimidate you," she told DW, noting that the financial bias still favors male candidates. Women comprise roughly 51% of Zambia's population but hold only about 15% of parliamentary seats, and fewer than 20% of political leadership positions. Leah Diana Mitaba, publicity secretary of the Non‑Governmental Coordinating Council, warns that these figures "demonstrate that Zambia remains far from achieving the 50:50 gender representation envisaged in the Constitution, the SADC Protocol on Gender and Development, the African Union Agenda 2063 and the UN Sustainable Development Goals." Girls Gone Political, a civil‑society group, campaigns for greater female participation. Its leader, Dorothy Mtanga, thinks more civic education is needed. "There's the need for sustained democratic civic education to ensure that more women are elected into office," she said. Judicial independence called into question This election also raises questions about the independence of Zambia's judiciary. In 2024, President Hichilema suspended three Constitutional Court judges who ruled in favor of his rival, former President Edgar Lungu. Lawyer Linda Kasonde argued that "judicial independence is the ability to adjudicate on any matter, without fear or favor, regardless of the stakes involved in the case." In practice, opposition lawyers think the executive is trying to interfere with justice delivery. Kasonde identifies two recent concerns. First, an executive‑approved salary increase for judges that bypassed the constitutional emoluments commission. "The government increased salaries for judicial officers in 2025 outside the proper procedure, raising questions about whether the process was independent," she told DW. Second, the appointment of 16 new judges in early 2026, many of whom hail from the incumbent's strongholds. "These appointments call into question whether any decisions that will be made regarding the elections will be done independently," lawyer Kasonde concluded. Amnesty International says Zambian laws including the Public Order Act and cybercrime legislation have been weaponized to restrict dissent, opposition gatherings and freedom of expression. It also warns that the increasing use of criminal charges against government critics could have a chilling effect on political expression. Chief Justice Mumba Malila recently reassured the public. "The judiciary stands ready to discharge its constitutional responsibility, independently, professionally and within the strict timelines established by the law," he said. Critics, however, maintain that true independence requires full structural and financial autonomy from the executive. Continuity or change? Zambia's status as one of the region's stable multi‑party democracies in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) means that this election will influence regional democratic norms. The country's ability to host a peaceful transition or renewal of power is a barometer for neighboring states, especially after recent defeats of incumbents in Botswana and Malawi. Polls will be open from 6:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Zambians will elect a president, National Assembly members, mayors, councilors, and council chairs. This election holds the potential to either consolidate President Hichilema's reform agenda or usher in a new administration. This article was compiled from several DW video reports covering Zambia's 2026 general election

item.title: How one German city is preparing for climate extremes
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.30
In October 2023, the worst storm surge in more than 150 years hit the Baltic Sea coast. It destroyed dikes, collapsed coastal cliffs and devastated marinas in the northern German state of Schleswig-Holstein and parts of southern Denmark. The catastrophic surge wiped away 2.68 meters (8.79 feet) of coastal bluff in Kiel, a port city and Schleswig-Holstein's capital. That was more than four times the yearly average lost over the previous two decades. Human-caused climate change is supercharging extreme weather such as storms. And in coastal cities like Kiel, the consequences are already impossible to ignore. "The impacts of climate change are hardly abstract in Kiel," said Martina Baum, who heads the city's climate adaptation division. "Since at least the 2023 storm surge, we have all been reminded of the profound effects it can have on us, on our daily lives, and on the environment around us." Those effects are forcing Kiel — among the first cities to declare a climate emergency back in 2019 — to rethink its design, and how it works. It has since become a front-runner in adapting to the realities of a changing climate, establishing Baum's division in 2025 to help make the city more resilient to weather extremes and adopting an adaptation plan in February 2026 to step up those measures. Is climate adaptation giving up on fighting climate change? For city officials like Baum, adaptation is not a substitute for cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet. Climate protection remains the first line of defense, because limiting warming will reduce future damage. "For a long time, there was hesitation to engage officially with the issue of climate change adaptation. I also felt uneasy about it at first, because it felt as though it would somehow take the pressure off climate protection efforts," Baum told DW. But the move to adaptation in Kiel reflects what's happening in other cities around the world from Santa Cruz in the US to Quezon City in the Philippines, as governments increasingly prepare for the impacts of heat, heavier rainfall and stronger storm surges that are already here. That doesn't mean climate protection and adaptation always align. Installing power-hungry air-conditioning in housing, daycare or senior centers, for instance, protects vulnerable people in heat waves. But it increases energy consumption, "which would run counter to climate protection goals," Baum said. "Even if we use renewable energy, demand is not yet covered by renewable sources 100% of the time, so any additional energy we consume will ultimately result in the emission of climate-damaging greenhouse gases," she added. Redesigning cities for unavoidable impacts While AC will sometimes be necessary, Kiel is working on solutions that cool the city naturally. It's adding vegetation to building facades, redesigning a park to channel cooler air into the city center, and making it easier for residents to access permits, information and grants for adaptation projects. The city is also testing which tree species can survive future conditions. A decade ago, Kiel planted five specimens each of 20 different species to find out which can best withstand heat, drought and salt spray from the nearby Baltic Sea. Trees provide shade, cool streets by roughly 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) and improve air quality, but not every species will thrive as the climate changes. "There is no one-size-fits-all climate tree; different sites require different tree species," said Nicole Holz, who works in the department responsible for the city's green spaces. The research requires patience. "It's going to take some 20, 30 years until you get some real results," said Petra Holtappel, head of the same department. Living differently: No more daytime soccer? Adapting to climate change will also require changes to daily life, said Baum. Children, for example, may no longer be able to play soccer tournaments at 3 p.m. because it's too hot. Although Kiel is getting warmer, it is expected to fare better than much hotter cities in Southern or Central Europe when it comes to heat. Still, the city is vulnerable to more storm surges and heavy rain and needs more retention areas to manage all that excess water. The city is dredging the park's pond to store stormwater during heavy rainfall, but is also exploring other ideas. "One idea is what's known as multi-use design, meaning that in future, a soccer pitch could be built slightly lower than the surrounding area. During periods of heavy rain, water could then be directed there and allowed to gradually infiltrate into the ground or evaporate," Baum said. The downside is the pitch might be unusable for up to 60 days a year, she added. But residents would need accept that, said Baum, who emphasized the need for greater public debate about adaptation measures. How to reach people who don't think about the climate? Helping residents understand those trade-offs and what's at stake is part of Annafried Stürmer's work. Stürmer organizes educational events, leads public excursions with scientists and attends neighborhood fairs to meet people who might not otherwise engage with climate issues. At Kiel Week in June, the world's biggest annual sailing event, Stürmer displayed a map showing city flood risk from extreme rainfall. "People often find that interesting, because it doesn't immediately seem like it's connected to climate change. Instead, the initial reaction is , 'Wow, if we get one of those intense heavy rainfall events, my house could be in serious trouble,' or 'My backyard could end up flooded,'" Stürmer said. Stürmer has often found it easier to talk about climate adaptation than about climate change, because the former is more tangible. "It's easier to talk about the need for a better-developed sewer system to handle heavy rainfall, or about planting different types of trees and vegetation, than it is to talk about reducing CO2 emissions," Stürmer told DW. Recent record heat waves have made the adaptation conservation more urgent too. "People noticed that it hadn't been as hot before," she said, adding residents increasingly recognize the need to protect children, the elderly, pregnant women and outdoor workers. Climate adaptation not 'optional' Even with growing public awareness of the need for adaptation, funding remains a problem in cash-strapped Kiel. Still seen as optional, climate action can quickly come under pressure when budgets tighten. "I disagree with the idea that climate adaptation and climate action are optional responsibilities. I keep asking myself: what are the alternatives?" Baum said. "After all, it has been demonstrated time and again that investing in climate adaptation and climate mitigation will simply pay off." Edited by: Jennifer Collins

item.title: Germany news: Some shipping stops as Rhine hits new lows
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.24
What you need to know These updates have been closed. Thank you for joining us. Here's a roundup of the biggest stories hitting the headlines in Germany on Tuesday, August 11. - Economic experts expect cuts to industrial production because of reduced cargo shipping on the Rhine river - All shipping past the town of Kaub has now stopped due to record low levels - Germany is reintroducing standing room tickets for national team games - Wildfires caused the temporary closure of a major autobahn in northern Germany - The number of children involved in road accidents has increased Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. Germany brings back standing tickets for international games In non-drought-related news, Germany's football federation has announced it is bringing back standing tickets for national team matches for the first time in more than 25 years. The German Football Association (DFB) said the tickets will already be available for incoming coach Jürgen Klopp's first home games, against Greece in Augsburg on September 27 and Serbia in Munich on October 1. Standing areas will also be available at both men's and women's national team and Under-21 home matches. DFB president Bernd Neuendorf said there had been strong demand from supporters for standing areas at international matches. "We have therefore campaigned within UEFA in recent years for the return of standing areas at internationals and tournaments," he said. "Standing areas are an integral part of fan culture and the stadium experience in Germany," DFB President Bernd Neuendorf said in a statement. "Our dialogue with fans has shown us just how strong the desire for standing areas at international matches is." UEFA had long required all-seater arrangements for its competitions, meaning standing sections routinely used in German domestic football could not be used for UEFA matches. In 2022, UEFA began testing the return of standing areas in selected countries, including Germany. Germany has a long tradition of standing terraces, with Borussia Dortmund's famous South Stand, the "Yellow Wall," holding almost 25,000 supporters. Drought also pressuring fuel prices, especially at a local level Shallow rivers are also impacting fuel and diesel prices at filling stations, particularly in the Rhine's heartland in western Germany. Germany's largest motoring club, the ADAC, said that the Rhine's low levels were pushing prices up at the pumps, because the freight barges on the Rhine are well suited to the transport of oil, gasoline and diesel. Their limited capacity was increasing "logistics costs for the transport of fuels and certain products, drastically in some cases," the ADAC's fuel market expert Christian Laberer said. Laberer said that fuel delivery varied around the country, and was achieved using rivers, but also a "network of seaports, refineries, pipelines as well as rail and road transport." Therefore, he said, the water levels' effects were being felt in a pronounced manner in some areas than others. Fuel prices have been highly labile for most of the year in Germany anyway amid the war in Iran and the wider conflicts in the Middle East, with costs currently more than one-quarter higher than they were at the start of the year. Hesse joins states allowing Sunday trucking to compensate for dry rivers The state of Hesse, home to the financial capital Frankfurt, has joined the ranks of German states to make use of an amnesty for heavy goods vehicle (HGV) transit on Sundays and bank holidays. The measure will come into effect this weekend. Typically all truck freight transport is banned on German roads on Sundays and public holidays, regardless of where it is coming from or going to. Some exceptions do apply for deliveries of perishable goods. The federal government has allowed states to opt in to exemptions on these rules given that several rivers are much less effective freight corridors at present. Prior to Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland, Schleswig-Holstein and the city state of Hamburg had all relaxed the rules. Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria and Mecklenburg Western-Pomerania also all plan to allow HGV freight as of this weekend. Saxony has taken a different approach so far, rejecting the idea of blanket permission and instead saying it would consider issuing special permits for certain transport. Some shipping stops on Rhine as level keeps dropping New record-low water levels have been measured on the Rhine, a vital transport waterway, with some cargo vessel owners stopping shipping on river sections in the south. The inland navigation agency WSV reported that the gauge at Kaub, near Koblenz, had fallen to an all-time low of 15 centimeters (5.9 inches) on Tuesday, indicating that the river depth is about 115 centimeters at its deepest point . A commodity trader told the Reuters news agency that it was "no longer to book cargo shipments on the Rhine past Kaub." "Most sailings there have stopped," the trader said. Traders said that sailings on northern sections of the river were continuing. Germany, along with much of Europe, has experienced a series of heat waves and a long period without meaningful rainfall this summer, leading to low water levels in several rivers. The situation is having not only an environmental but also an economic impact, with companies that are reliant on goods normally transported via water suffering supply shortfalls. The ships that are still sailing are carrying much lighter loads than usual and at higher prices. In pictures: Rhine water levels hit historic low Endurance athlete to swim 200 kilometers from Frankfurt to Cologne for child water safety The 31-year-old endurance swimmer Nathalie Pohl took to the water in the Main River in Frankfurt on Tuesday at the start of a planned 200-kilometer (125-mile) swim to Cologne. Pohl intends to swim via the Main and Rhine rivers to her destination over four days in a feat aimed at drawing attention to the importance of safe swimming, particularly for children. According to figures from the German Livesaving Association (DLRG), at least 261 people have died by drowning this year up to the end of July. The action is intended to raise money for swimming projects and education. Swim not without risks She is being accompanied by other swimmers who will put in one-hour sessions between her two-hour stints in the water. Ahead of the start, Pohl showed herself unfazed by the possibility that low water levels in the Rhine could mean a weaker current at her and her team's back. "Enough water is there and it shouldn't be a problem," she told the German DPA news agency, saying, however, that she hoped the algae that thrive in low water would not affect her health. Pohl received a special permit for her action, with German authorities fundamentally warning against swimming in large rivers. "Ultimately, something can always happen," she said, while stressing that she and her team had a comprehensive safety concept. What you need to know about low river water levels Water levels in several rivers in Germany, including the Rhine, have hit record lows that are well below normal for this time of year, causing severe disruptions to river traffic, with ships cutting their loads by about 80%. The water shortage comes during a prolonged dry period in Germany, accompanied by frequent heat waves, both of which are attributed by scientists partly to the effects of human-induced climate change. But why is the situation so serious for Germany, and what are the key terms in connection with low water levels? The Rhine: A vital transport waterway The Rhine has been used as a transport corridor for much of western Europe since Roman times. It is the most important waterway in Europe, connecting industrial regions in Germany, Switzerland and other countries with big North Sea ports, including Rotterdam in the Netherlands. Although only one in 10 tons of freight in Germany is transported via rivers such as the Rhine, they are much used for certain goods, including ore, oil, chemical products and coal. As a result, industries that depend on these for their production are likely to be forced to cut their output, as not only is supply reduced in the current situation, but transport prices have also gone up massively. What are river gauge measurements? The depth of water in German rivers is measured by gauges (Pegel) situated at strategic points on their course. These gauges, which are mostly located near the banks of a river, measure the depth of the river over an arbitrarily selected baseline. This means the measurements are only an indication of the actual navigable depth, which can be much more. For instance, although the gauge at the town of Kaub currently measures 16 cm (6.3 inches), the depth of the river in the channel used by shipping there is around 129 cm. Why is the gauge at Kaub so important? Kaub is situated on the Middle Rhine between St. Goar and Budenheim. This section of river is seen as a chokepoint for shipping on the Rhine, as the navigable channel is not as well developed as in other places. It has also long been used since 1856 as a key location to measure low water levels in the Rhine. The previous lowest measurement in Kaub was 25 cm (9.8 inches) on October 22, 2018. The present measurement of 16 cm is thus already a historic low — and it is expected to sink to single figures in the next few days. Child road accidents rising steadily More children were killed or injured in road accidents in 2025 than in in the previous year. That represents a renewed rise in road deaths and injuries affecting children since a decline during the coronavirus pandemic, statistics show. Altogether 29,270 children under the age of 15 were injured in traffic accidents in Germany last year, a 7% increase over 2024, the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) says. The number of children killed in such accidents also rose from 53 in 2024 to 74 in 2025. Of those fatalities, 30 were children under 6, well up on the number of children in that age group that were killed in 2024 (18). The largest increase in deaths was seen in children travelling in cars (21 to 31). The number of children killed on their bicycles in 2025 rose to 13 from 8 the previous year, while 4 were killed riding e-scooters, compared with none in 2024. Most of the children involved in road traffic accidents in 2025 were riding a bicycle (34%). Altogether 31% were in a car, 20% were on foot and 8% were travelling on an e-scooter when the accidents occurred "On average, a child was injured or killed in a road traffic accident every 18 minutes in 2025," Destatis said. Germany needs planned intelligence agency reforms, top politician says The chairman of the parliamentary panel overseeing Germany's secret services, Marc Henrichmann, has defended the new powers planned for intelligence agencies. "The latest security incident at the Leipzig freight airport has shown once again that we are dealing with a new quality of hybrid threats," Henrichmann told the daily Rheinische Post. An explosives-laden unmanned aerial vehicle was flown into the airport last week. Henrichmannsaid that cyber attacks, sabotage and unauthorized drone overflights were "now part of a reality for which we have to be better prepared." For this reason, he said, both the foreign intelligence agency (BND) and the domestic intelligence agency (BfV) needed the "necessary legal and technical options" to detect threats early on and identify their sources. The reform plans have met with criticism from civil liberty activists. The Society for Civil Rights (GFF) has voiced fears that they could lead to a "massive increase in power for intelligence agencies. "The BND and BfV are to be allowed to intervene profoundly in basic rights with expanded use of government spyware, AI analyses practically without protective measures, access to private video cameras and even hack-backs although the legal hurdles often remain vague and too low," the organization's Kai Dittmann said. He called for the draft bill to be thoroughly revised, calling it "unconstitutional in many parts." The draft reform bill is set to be approved by the German Cabinet on Wednesday. Autobahn reopens after closure because of wildfire A highway in the northern state of Lower Saxony has reopened after being closed for over 12 hours as wildfire smoke dangerously reduced visibility. Police closed the A7 autobahn to traffic between Göttingen and Kassel on Monday afternoon after thick smoke from the fire near Hannoversch Münden engulfed the road. A police spokeswoman said some clean-up operations on a section of the motorway went on until the early hours of Tuesday morning but that both sides could now be used. Low water in Rhine will cause production cuts — IW research institute The reduction in cargo being shipped via the Rhine because of low water levels will lead companies to cut production, a leading economic research institute reports. "Transport routes south of Kaub are now threatening to become completely severed, meaning the Rhine is cut in two," Thomas Puls, the transport expert from the German Economic Institute (IW) told the daily Rheinische Post. "Because neither road nor rail are able to take the goods needed, the most likely reaction of primary industries will be to reduce production," he said. This assessment appeared to be confirmed by a spokesman for the chemical company Covestro, who told the paper that the shortfalls in supply caused by the disruption to Rhine shipping was already affecting production. The spokesman said that the current lifting of a ban on trucks using the motorway on Sundays would be of only temporary benefit. "Ship transport via the Rhine can barely be compensated on the road, as a cargo vessel that can carry 1,500 tons is the equivalent of around 60 trucks," he said. "So ship transport cannot be completely shifted to roads." The record low water levels on the Rhine caused by a prolonged shortage of rainfall in Germany mean that ships are currently able to carry only around a fifth of the load they usually transport. Welcome to our coverage A warm guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn! And, as has so often been the case recently, that very river is at the focus of our reporting from Germany as low water levels cause major disruption to cargo shipping and thus potentially to the industries that depend on it. Another main topic is the threat to national security from hybrid forms of warfare, as reflected in recent drone incidents at sensitive sites. The government is moving to give intelligence agencies new powers to combat this threat, something that some see as a danger to civil liberties. And we also take a look at statistics showing that road accidents involving children are on the rise again after a reduction during the coronavirus pandemic.

item.title: Disrupted monsoons force India to face climate threat
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.14
India's southwest monsoon usually arrives around June, bringing most of the country's annual rainfall, and begins to retreat by September. Its timing and intensity have always varied, but the broad pattern was predictable enough for farmers, cities and businesses to plan around it. Now, this natural rhythm increasingly seems like a thing of the past. More than 100 people have been killed across India since late July as heavy monsoon rains triggered floods, landslides and lightning strikes. The northeastern state of Assam has borne the brunt, with more than 120,000 people affected by flooding. Kerala, Jammu and Kashmir, Bihar and Jharkhand have also reported deaths and widespread disruption. The problem is not necessarily that India is receiving more rain. It is the way the rain is arriving: longer dry spells are followed by short bursts of intense rainfall that can overwhelm rivers, drainage systems and hillsides. El Nino has added to this year's variability but scientists say the longer-term changes are being driven by a changing climate. Have the monsoons entered a new era? Akshay Deoras, a senior research scientist with the UK's National Centre for Atmospheric Science and the University of Reading, cautions against describing the Indian monsoon as having entered "a fundamentally different regime." "Active and break spells have always been part of the monsoon. What appears to be changing is their intensity," Deoras told DW. He pointed out a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, making active spells, or periods of intense rainfall, more intense. Madhavan Nair Rajeevan, a climate scientist and former secretary in the Ministry of Earth Sciences, says the change is visible in the behaviour of the monsoon itself. Average seasonal rainfall, he said, has not shown a systematic long-term change and the monsoon remains a robust natural phenomenon. But the timing, intensity and distribution of rainfall are all noticeably different. "The characteristics of the Indian monsoon have changed fundamentally," Rajeevan told DW. "We are witnessing an increase in short-duration rainfall extremes, longer dry spells, and changes in the frequency, intensity and distribution of monsoon weather systems." He believes the rise in extreme rainfall is more than natural variability. "It represents a structural shift in the monsoon system," he said. Villages and cities both at risk India's farmers depend heavily on the timing of rainfall. Long dry spells can disrupt sowing and reduce soil moisture and intense rain can wash away fields and damage crops. India's cities are also struggling due to rapid construction, as new roads and buildings leave less land to absorb water, thus interfering with natural drainage. Moreover, after weeks of dry weather, hard, dry soil absorbs less water. When heavy rain finally arrives, more of it floods the rivers and drains instead of replenishing groundwater. India not stepping up to extreme weather hazard "The greatest risks increasingly come from short periods of very intense rainfall," Deoras told DW, warning that India's infrastructure is increasingly out of step with this changing threat. Deoras says drainage systems and flood management are still too often designed around historical seasonal rainfall averages rather than the short, high-impact events that cause the greatest disruption. He noted that forecasting has improved, but knowing that extreme rain is coming is only useful if authorities act on the warning. Warnings, he said, need to translate into "timely, impact-based decisions" such as changing school schedules, restricting travel or closing off vulnerable areas before heavy rain arrives. Ritwick Dutta, an environmental lawyer and managing trustee of the Legal Initiative for Forest and Environment, says the problem goes beyond extreme weather itself. "It is now scientifically accepted that climate change leads to erratic rainfall patterns: high rainfall over a few days followed by long dry periods during the monsoon," Dutta told DW. "These trends have been compounded by the fact that the decision-making process in India fails to consider climate change while planning construction projects." Dutta points to the western city of Pune, where a study by the state government and the Energy and Resources Institute projects a 37% increase in rainfall by 2030. Still, Dutta says this projection has not been adequately incorporated into the city's planning, including its riverfront development. "Dams, embankments and roads are all likely to suffer major damage due to climate change, and yet we proceed as though climate change is a matter to be discussed only in conferences and workshops," Dutta said. "We are, in effect, 'weaponizing the environment'," Dutta said. Dutta says India's environmental clearance system does not require climate change to be systematically factored into project decisions. "The concept of 'climate proofing' does not exist here," he said. Thousands killed in last year's monsoon The Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) found that extreme weather affected India on 331 of 334 monitored days in 2025, or 99% of the period assessed. More than 4,000 people died, about 3,000 during the monsoon, while at least 30 states and union territories experienced extreme weather simultaneously for eight consecutive months. Sunita Narain, director general of the CSE, argues that adaptation therefore needs to become part of the country's development strategy. "Climate change is no longer a future threat. It is already here in the form of extreme heat, extreme rainfall and increasingly destructive weather events," Narain told DW. "The challenge is no longer proving the science, but redesigning our economy and infrastructure to survive it," she added. "Cities, roads, drainage systems and water infrastructure can no longer be designed for yesterday's climate." Every investment, she says, must be planned for a future of more intense and unpredictable weather. In her reckoning, India must stop treating each flood as an isolated disaster and start planning for a climate in which such extremes are no longer exceptional. What can be done against extreme weather? India is facing a whole new pattern of extreme weather. It can record a rainfall deficit nationally while individual regions are underwater. Farmers can go weeks without useful rain and then lose crops in a few hours. Cities can prepare for an average monsoon and still be overwhelmed by one extraordinary downpour. "The focus now needs to move beyond documenting and discussing these changes towards developing and implementing effective, sector-specific adaptation strategies," climate scientist and former Indian official Rajeevan said. That means better flood management in cities, changes in agricultural practices, stronger water-storage systems and infrastructure designed around short-duration extreme rainfall rather than historical averages. India cannot control the monsoon or El Nino and it cannot stop global warming on its own. It can decide, however, where it builds, how it builds and if its new infrastructure is designed for the climate of its future. Edited by: Darko Janjevic

item.title: Hungary's parliament elects Orban critic as new president
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.89
Hungary's parliament voted in Andras Baka, formerly the head of the Supreme Court, as the country's next president on Tuesday. The symbolic step is part of new Prime Minister Peter Magyar's sweeping efforts to dismantle the legacy of former premier Viktor Orban after winning April's general elections. Baka was a staunch critic of Orban who was removed from his Supreme Court role during the former PM's tenure. Now, he will replace Tamas Sulyok, a president appointed by Orban, whose term in office was shortened via constitutional amendment in order to remove him from the largely ceremonial role. What happened in Tuesday's parliamentary vote? The vote in parliament to appoint Baka was always likely to be a formality, given the massive majority that Magyar's conservative, pro-European TISZA party holds in the chamber. It went almost entirely along party lines, 140 lawmakers voted in favor and six voted against. TISZA holds 141 seats. Orban's right-wing populist Fidesz party, which has 52 lawmakers, boycotted the vote in protest — but did so knowing it would be powerless to prevent Baka's appointment. Who is Andras Baka? Baka, 73, is a jurist and politician who was briefly a member of parliament from 1990 to 1991. He spent almost 20 years as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), before returning to Hungary in 2009 to become president of its Supreme Court. In December 2011, not long after Orban returned to power as prime minister after a stint in opposition, he was removed from his role three years before his term was set to expire and sidelined from public life in Hungary. Magyar said Baka's life served "as an example of commitment to the democratic rule of law and constitutional principles" as the central European country needs to be "guided back onto the path of the rule of law and constitutional governance." Why was Baka's appointment and his predecessor's removal contentious? Baka's appointment prompted protests from Fidesz, but also some critical comments elsewhere in Hungary, with some rights watchdogs likening the removal of Tamas Sulyok to the "illiberal" practices of the Orban-era. Sulyok, appointed in 2024, was deemed an Orban ally. Magyar used his two-thirds majority in parliament — which he holds thanks to Hungary's winner-takes-all first-past-the-post electoral system, as Orban used to — to amend the constitution and bring his term to an early end. Fidesz and their nationalist KDNP allies in parliament had called this "tyrannical" and "illegitimate," while Magyar argued it was necessary to pursue the "system change" he promised amid April's landslide election victory. Magyar briefly tapped Hungarian national treasure and chess superstar Judit Polgar as a possible replacement president, but she quickly declined, saying she did not feel she had "the strength to take on the historic responsibility of uniting a divided nation," but pledging to do "everything in my power" to support a new, independent and respected president. What has Baka said about the process and his appointment? Baka himself had not criticized Sulyok's removal, despite the echoes of the mechanisms used to oust him in 2011. "In a country governed by the rule of law, such extraordinary measures cannot be used, but Hungary became a captured state under Orban," he told the AFP news agency last month. He said that state officials like Sulyok "were appointed not to restrain the government's power, but to ensure the political survival of the former system even after an electoral defeat." However, speaking in parliament on Tuesday, Baka seemed to strike a conciliatory tone, even for supporters of the old regime. "There is one thing we certainly cannot do: we cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," he told parliament, vowing to "encourage public and professional debate, uphold [parliament's] openness and impartiality, and consistently insist that constitution-making must never again become the exclusive project of a single political force." Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Syria sentences Bashar Assad to death in absentia
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.29
A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced former President Bashar Assad to death in absentia. Assad was ousted in December 2024 after rebel forces swept into Damascus, ending more than five decades of rule by the Assad family. He and his family fled to Russia, where he was granted asylum, as Syria's new authorities began pursuing former officials over alleged crimes committed during the country's civil war. What did the court say about Assad? Assad was convicted of the crimes of "premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children, torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity." "The contribution of the criminal Bashar Assad to the crimes was that of the person ultimately responsible for decision-making, mobilizing state institutions to commit them," the judge said. The verdict was handed down by Damascus' Fourth Criminal Court and read out live on Syrian state television. Assad, born in 1965, became president in 2000 after the death of his father, Hafez Assad. He continued his family's decadeslong rule, maintaining the dominance of the Alawite minority in Sunni-majority Syria and the country's close alliance with Iran as well as hostility toward Israel and the US. The Syrian government has been demanding that Moscow extradite Assad. Assad's brother Maher and several other figures from the ousted government were also sentenced to death in absentia. They were convicted of premeditated murder and torture resulting in death. Assad's cousin sentenced in person In the same case, the court also handed the death penalty to Atef Najib, a senior security official under Assad's rule and a cousin of the former dictator. He was arrested while trying to flee the country in January 2025 and became one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial. Najib, a former Syrian army brigadier general, headed the Political Security Branch in the southern province of Daraa when the uprising against Assad's government began in 2011. He appeared in court under tight security, standing inside a cage in a prison uniform as the judge read out the sentence. The court convicted Najib of crimes including murder, the intentional killing of children under 15 and torture resulting in death, describing the acts as crimes against humanity.
