item.title: Dodge Just Revived One of Its Most Track-Ready Muscle Cars
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 2.04
Dodge Just Revived One of Its Most Track-Ready Muscle Cars The iconic American auto brand has unleashed a modern take on the Charger Super Bee. Plus, a new-age CD player, an affordable hiking backpack from Timberland and more. Dodge unleashed a modern take on one of its most iconic track-ready muscle cars, the Charger Super Bee. Hot off the launch of the gas-powered Charger earlier this year, the new Super Bee channels some of the model’s rich and performance-driven heritage. Much like the original Super Bee, the current one packs even more punch with an SAE-certified 600-horsepower rating, which is 50 more than the standard SIXPACK HO (High Output). The Super Bee also boasts beefier brakes, more aerodynamic enhancements, track-tuned suspension, and a lovely eye-catching exterior color palette to match it all. Step bars for that trail-ready stance. A matte black grille lettering kit for the full blackout look. A logo spare tire cover to make it unmistakably yours. Add the MOLLE grate system, and the swing gate becomes a gear locker built for your next overlanding run. Ford’s Bronco accessories don’t just look the part. They define the build, roof to bumper. Now through August 25, save 25% on select Bronco® and Bronco Sport® Accessories, up to $1,000, with the code BRONCO25. Best known for its signature boots, you probably wouldn’t expect that Timberland would be a brand to get into EDC, outdoor adventure or travel. But the brand’s Heritage 27-Liter Backpack says otherwise. Inspired by classic rucksacks, this pack is constructed from lightweight polyester (which is naturally weather-resistant), has a classic combination of a cinch opening and a flip top closure, boasts a padded back panel and straps, has an internal laptop sleeve and so much more. It’s also done up in the brand’s most iconic color combination. Yet, it comes in at just $80, which is quite the steal. Rezvani’s Beast X represents the pinnacle of the brand’s on-road efforts, a brutally exclusive hypercar that’s set to number just five units strong. Derived from a C8 Corvette, it packs a custom-built 6.2-liter V8 with fully forged internals and a trick all-wheel drive system. On the road, this means it puts down a claimed 1,560 horsepower, and Rezvani says it can hit 60 mph in a mere 1.9 seconds. In keeping with the striking looks, it’s dripping in carbon fiber and other exotic material details. Syitren’s RM1 flips the conventional CD player inside out, literally. The dual-layer transparent acrylic frame leaves the spinning disc, optical pickup and electronics fully exposed, turning playback into kinetic wall art. Mounting flat against a wall or standing on a desk, the device outputs audio via Bluetooth 5.3 or a 3.5mm jack and runs for six to eight hours on a 2,000mAh rechargeable battery. Its perfect for CD enthusiasts ready to put their favorite discs on full display. Part of Raide’s new female-first toolkit, this women’s-specific running belt is designed to help women run further. The LF 2L Running Belt offers the same carry capacity and structure as the brand’s standard LF 2L, but is constructed with an increased taper between the top and bottom hems that accommodates a wider variety of body shapes. The belt has been adjusted to offer a full opening so it can be wrapped around the hips, rather than pulled on. Additionally, a 650mL HydraPak flask with a locking cap is included with every belt. Raide’s new release sold out of sizes XS and S on release, and the rest of the size run is almost gone at the time of this writing. Norton teams up with motorsport and lifestyle brand Peaceful Research for an eye-popping 1 of 1 take on its Manx R superbike. The bike features a pink paint scheme accented with a peace sign (naturally) on the fairing, backed up by a 1,200cc V4 engine making 203 horsepower at 11,500 rpm and 96 Ib-ft of torque at 9,000 rpm, of course. No word yet whether the bike will actually be available for purchase, but the accompanying collab T-shirt, hoodie and hat are presumably much more affordable.

item.title: Archaeologists Thought a Mass Grave of 79 Shackled Men Held Foreign Invaders. They Were Wrong
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.46
In 2016, archaeologists in Athens uncovered an Ancient Greek mass grave full of men buried in a heartbreakingly vulnerable position: with their wrists shackled and raised over their heads. We now have a better sense of who they were.Â Â Researchers conducted isotopic analyses on 66 men from the so-called Esplanada grave, which dates back to the Archaic Period (~700 to 460 BCE), and discovered something surprisingâmost were from the surrounding region of Attica. In other words, they were locals, according to a study published last month in the Journal of Archaeological Science. The findings shed light on the identities of the victims but also hold broader implications for our understanding of the political and societal dynamics taking place in Athens right before ancient Greeceâs famous Classical Period (479-323 BCE).Â Local or foreign victims? All the major themes related to the Classical Periodâsuch as, most famously, democracyâactually develop out of the Archaic Period. âThatâs the first time democracy takes place in Athens,â Julianne Stamer, a bioarchaeologist at Arizona State University and lead author of the study, told Gizmodo. But not everyone agreed with this form of rule, and archaic Athens saw intense disagreement over whether the future city-state should be presided over by an aristocratic tyrant or the public. Still, when the Esplanada grave came to light with its 79 men arranged in three parallel rows, researchers werenât sure what to make of it. Were they victims of these domestic conflicts? Or perhaps defeated foreign invaders? To settle the matter, Stamer and her colleagues turned to radiogenic strontium analysis.Â âStrontum is an element that is found in the ground in relative abundance based on how old the rocks are and what kind of rocks they are,â Stamer explained. âBecause strontium isotopes get into our water and into our food, we all have some strontium isotopes in our teeth and bones,â she added. By measuring those isotopes, âwe can tell where people are from based on the geology of the surrounding area.âÂ Very few outsiders The team conducted radiogenic strontium analysis on 66 of the Esplanada men as well as 97 other people from the broader Phaleron burial ground that includes the mass grave. Their work revealed that the vast majority of them were locals. Among the men in the mass grave specifically, the analyses identified only two of them as outsiders.Â âWe found that most people have a strontium isotope signature that appears to be from the wider Attica region,â said Stamer, bolstering the theory of them being victims of internal political violence. Still, âwe were very surprised about that because in this period, Athens and Greece in general are becoming more interconnected. We have a lot more trade going on.â This dynamic is, once again, a precursor to the sort of connections that later contribute to making Athens a mighty Classical power.Â The Archaic burial ground itself is strongly associated with trade and travel. The Phaleron burial ground is right next to Athensâ ancient port, Phaleron, from which it takes its name. And yet the people buried there donât represent the sort of diversity one would expect from the years leading up to Athensâ extremely well-connected Classical Period.Â Archaic dynamics Not that Classical Athenians particularly liked diversity, either. In fact, they had very strict citizenship laws, but historians donât know if this was true during the previous Archaic Period, too. The isotopic analyses indicate that Attica might not have received many immigrants during this period. Perhaps this represents a dislike of foreigners during the Archaic Period that continues into the Classical Period despite the intense trade going on.Â Moving forward, Stamer and the team are taking an even deeper dive into the identities of those buried at Phaleron, including what they ate.Â By revealing where the Esplanada men were from, the recent study provides additional clues about what social and political life in Athens might have been like in the centuries preceding its most famous time period. And itâs pretty clear that it had some seriously dark moments whether or not you were an immigrant.Â

item.title: This Satellite Will Literally Breathe Air to Stay in Orbit
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.03
A new type of propulsion system could allow satellites to fly closer to Earth than ever before without being dragged down by the planet’s atmosphere. Spanish startup Kreios Space developed an air-breathing electric propulsion system that collects residual gases from the atmosphere, like oxygen and nitrogen, and uses them as propellant for a satellite’s thrusters. The new technology would allow satellites to stay in very low Earth orbit (VLEO), circling our planet at roughly 60 miles to 250 miles (100 to 400 kilometers) above the surface. The air-breathing system will be put to its first test in space during an upcoming mission in 2028, Kreios recently announced. Breathe in, breathe out Satellites flying in very low Earth orbit face severe atmospheric drag, rapidly decaying their orbit and pulling them down to a fiery death. For satellites to remain in VLEO, their propulsion systems would require large amounts of propellant to counter atmospheric drag. That’s not ideal for space missions, as it creates a satellite that is too heavy and expensive to launch. For Kreios’ air-breathing electric propulsion, the idea is to maintain that low altitude without the need for any propellant on board the satellite. Instead, the propulsion system scoops up air from Earth’s upper atmosphere, heats it up to ionize it, and expels it to generate thrust. The company has tested a prototype of its new propulsion system in a lab in 2021. For its first in-orbit demonstration, Kreios is using a microsatellite bus by Lithuania-based Kongsberg NanoAvionics to carry the air-breathing propulsion system to space. The upcoming mission is designed to validate the new technology, take measurements of the surrounding environment, and capture sub-meter resolution images in the visible and near-infrared (VNIR) spectral range. How low There are several advantages to satellites flying in VLEO as they can gather sharper, higher-resolution images of Earth, offer stronger signals, and require smaller parts for the same level of performance as those operating in low Earth orbit. VLEO is also significantly less crowded than low Earth orbit, with fewer satellites and less space debris zipping around at high speeds. âKreios is building the satellites that make sustained operations in Very Low Earth Orbit possible,” AdriÃ¡n Senar, CEO of Kreios Space, said in a statement. “By enabling satellites to fly lower, longer, and more efficiently, we are enabling higher-resolution Earth observation, much better satellite communications, more responsive and accurate missions, and a more sustainable orbital infrastructure.” China has also shown recent interest in VLEO, establishing a national industry alliance designed to demonstrate sustainable operations of satellites closer to Earth.

item.title: This Deadly Drug-Resistant Fungus Can Lurk in Your Skin. Scientists Just Discovered How
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.83
The fungus Candida auris is one of the scarier emerging diseases out there, but scientists may have just uncovered a key secret to its survival that could allow us to fight back. Researchers at the University of California-San Francisco studied how the fungal pathogen behaved on the skin of mice. Compared to other related fungi, C. auris triggered a distinct response from the skin’s immune cells, they foundâone that enabled it to easily hunker down in hair follicles. The discovery could lead to new treatments that can clear the fungus from our skin before it becomes a life-threatening problem, the researchers say. “These results suggest that C. auris exploits a distinctive immune axis to persist,” the researchers wrote in their paper, published last week in the journal Science. The resistant, deadly fungus Doctors in Japan first discovered C. auris inside a personâs ear in 2009. Since then, it’s become one of the most urgent superbug threats in the world, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The fungus is uniquely adept at evolving resistance to the most common medications used to treat fungal infections; some strains have even been pan-resistant to every type of antifungal we have available today. Another insidious feature of C. auris is its ability to easily colonize the skin of healthy people, something that isn’t normally seen with other Candida species. Though most people carrying C. auris on the skin will never fall ill as a result, the fungus can cause problematic and often life-threatening bloodstream infections when a person’s immune system weakens. Carriers can also spread the fungus within hospitals or other places occuped by medically vulnerable individuals, such as nursing homes (this can happen through direct contact or even just shared medical equipment and room surfaces). The UCSF researchers were hoping to find out how and why C. auris can survive so well on skin, so they conducted experiments in the lab and with mice. They compared C. auris to its cousin Candida albicans, a species that can also cause human fungal infections but isn’t quite talented at persisting on skin. For starters, they found that C. auris loves to colonize hair follicles in particular. What’s more, theseÂ two fungi generated two very different kinds of immune responses from the mice. C. albicans tended to trigger higher levels of interleukin-17 (IL-17), a protein known for its role in tamping down fungal infections.Â C. auris, however, triggered the release of interferon gamma, which is typically used to help fight off viral infections. This wayward response not only blocked the release of IL-17, but it also appeared to slow down the replacement of hair follicle cells, both of which allowed C. auris to make itself nice and cozy in its hiding spot. Further experiments found evidence that C. auris triggers interferon gamma by changing its outer cell walls to expose more chitin, a tough sugar-based molecule commonly seen in fungi as well as the shells of insects and other invertebrates. “Our study helps explain why, once C. auris colonizes the skin, it can be so difficult to eliminate: the fungus senses cues from the skin environment and responds by remodeling itself in ways that favor survival, including reshaping the local immune response to promote its persistence within the skin and hair follicles,” lead study author Dean Merrill, a dermatologist and professor at UCSF, told Gizmodo. How this might help fight the superbug Merill is careful to note that C. auris poses little threat to the vast majority of people carrying it on their skin. That said, though still rare in general, annual C. auris infections have steadily climbed. This year so far, there have been more than 3,400 cases reported in the U.S., putting it on pace to surpass last year’s total. Should the team’s research be further validated (including studies in people), it could provide some important insights into the hardy fungus. While many scientists are actively working to develop new antifungals and vaccines that can treat or prevent invasive infections from C. auris and other fungi, we need all the help we can get. So the UCSF team is hopeful their work can eventually spur research into other strategies for fending off these superbugs. “Understanding these adaptations gives us new potential targets for developing better ways to clear C. auris from the skin and prevent its spread,” said Merill. It might be possible to develop proactive interventions that can nudge our skin’s defense toward the right immune response, for instance, or to otherwise prevent C. auris from tricking the immune system. And simply studying C. auris more might help us learn how to suppress its transformation from a harmless skin passenger to a killer drug-resistant germ, the researchers say.

item.title: OpenAI’s Only Ethicist Reportedly Left Last Month. She Wasn’t Replaced
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.59
OpenAIâs head ethicist, ChloÃ© Bakalar, quietly left the company at some point in July after having been hired the previous August. Before working at OpenAI, she was Metaâs chief ethicist, and established AI ethics policies for Instagram and Facebook, according to a story by the Financial Times. The FTâs anonymous source apparently told that paper that Bakalar specialized in âethical approaches to model development, how humans interact with AI and debate over machine consciousness.â Whoever that source is, they apparently also said Bakalar hadnât been replaced, and that she had been the sole dedicated ethicist at OpenAI. OpenAI is, in other words, reportedly now ethicist-free. In the present context, itâs remarkable to hear part of Bakalarâs relatively down-to-earth message to the 2023 Forbes Healthcare Summit during a panel on trust, given when she was still working at Meta: "The ability to make people feel heard and understood and seen, that's immensely important, especially in the healthcare field." ChloÃ© Bakalar, Ph.D., Chief Ethicist, Responsible AI (RAI) at @Meta, discussed generative AI and healthcare. #ForbesHealth pic.twitter.com/S8gmvOnwKl — Forbes (@Forbes) December 5, 2023 Publicly available LLMs were still pretty new at the time, and Bakalar was eager to point out that they were âstill prediction machines,â and not âemotive, feeling, entities.â Sentience and feeling, she opined, were absolutely not happening at the time. âWe are so far away from that,â she said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altmanâs tone with regard to the technological âsingularityâ has shifted a bit recently. He had previously suggested humanity was on the approachâwriting a blog post called âThe Gentle Singularityâ for instance, roughly two months before Bakalar was hired. But at the end of last month, in an appearance on a podcast called Relentless, Altman sounded more confident and forceful. “We are now, like, in the singularity,” he said, and added, “I’ve been waiting for this my whole life, and I think it’s going to be incredible, hugely positive, awesome for the world.” To be absolutely clear, statements that humanity is in the singularity wouldnât necessarily conflict with statements to the effect that LLMs arenât sentient. Definitions of the singularity vary wildly. In recent weeks, OpenAI has been front-and-center in a cascade of overlapping and bewildering news stories about AI safety and the governmentâs role in regulating it. Multiple OpenAI models famously âbroke containmentâ and hacked Hugging Face servers in pursuit of answers to an evaluation exercise. The Trump Administration announced, but did not detail, a rubric for the voluntary vetting of AI models. Perhaps relatedly, OpenAI reportedly plans to delay the release of a powerful new model, Astra, and according to the Information, Sam Altman personally traveled to Washington, D.C. to put Astra on display for policymakers. Bakalar is far from the only safety-adjacent OpenAI departure in the past few weeks. Head of Safety Systems Johannes Heidecke and Joshua Achiam, who has worn many hats as an OpenAI safety specialist, also left this summer. But as Iâve written before, safety at OpenAI involves a lot of churn.Â Â Last month, OpenAIâs Chief Research Officer Mark Chen gave a statement to Wired about an apparent new approach to safety in which such considerations sound like they’re sprinkled in throughout development. âItâs important that our safety work is integrated with frontier-model development, with an earlier and more direct role in shaping key model, product, and launch decisions.â When Gizmodo reached out to OpenAI with questions about Bakalarâs departureâincluding a request for confirmation that there is now no ethicist at OpenAIâa representative provided a statement that had previously been given to FT after its article was initially published: âWe’re thankful for Chloe’s contributions. AI ethics doesnât live with one owner or team at OpenAI, and ethical considerations are deeply embedded into the model building process driven by a number of teams across research.”

item.title: Turns Out Ancient Rome Took Tax Fraud Very Seriously
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.32
Befitting of its legacy and influence, the Roman Empire didnât play around with its laws, even by modern standards. For one, serious tax fraud was a crime punishable by death. That appears to have been the fate of a certain official or local dignitary around 480 CE, according to new findings from the European Research Councilâs STONE-MASTERS project. The discovery was announced in a statement from the University of Warsaw in Poland. The team found stone fragments with inscriptions in 2024, which at the time was attributed to a funeral verse commemorating a person of status. Closer inspections, however, revealed that the fragments were the missing parts of previous texts detailing a legal decision, namely a threat of execution, issued in 480 CE due to decades-long tax evasion in Anatolia, or modern-day Turkey. “As it turned out, the officials appointed to collect taxes there engaged in very bad practice,” PaweÅ Nowakowski, an archaeologist at the University of Warsaw involved in the latest work, explained in the statement (translated via Google Translate). “In practice, they most likely reported different, lower amounts in documents submitted to Constantinople, while collecting much more money from the local population. The difference went into their pockets.â The text doesn’t explicitly say that the execution was carried out. Contextually, however, it seems most likely that the envoy carrying the decree âarrived at the location and carried out his assigned taskâotherwise we would not have an inscription publishing the prefectâs decision,â Nowakowski added. The Roman IRS Economists have called the Roman conquests âinvestment opportunities.â New territories became sources of both resources and tax levies, while continued military campaigns were also funded by taxes. Unsurprisingly, tax collection wasnât perfect. In fact, according to the statement, archaeologists knew about the scandal mentioned in the latest discovery since the 19th century. Following the initial recovery of the stone fragments, the team recorded the individual letters carved into the stone and ran the record against a digital database. As a result, they were able to trace the text back to already known copies of the legal decision issued in 480 CE, according to the statement. “It concerned tax abuses in western Asia Minor [Anatolia],â Nowakowski explained. âIn practice, they most likely reported different, lower amounts in documents submitted to Constantinople, while collecting much more money from the local population. The difference went into their pockets.â More specifically, Roman central authorities received word about this fraudulent behavior as early as 465 CE, and a government official intervened but was âignored by the dishonest officials,â Nowakowski said. Then in 480 CE, the praetorian prefect sent an envoy to resolve the matter, threatening him with confiscation of his own property if he failed to fix it within three months. The corrupt officials themselves were threatened with something far worse: the death penalty. Real bad fraud That said, tax evasion penalties werenât typically this harsh. Known records from the era show that, between the 4th and 6th centuries, Roman emperors and officials issued at least 11 documents mandating accurate tax certificates. Archaeologists believe this could point to widespread abuse of tax laws in the era. None of them threatened death, however. “I think this can be interpreted as not so much about the gravity of the offense itself but also about opposing the imperial will and, in a sense, committing rebellion or lese-majestÃ© [injured majesty, meaning a crime against the state],â said Nowakowski. “It may also have been a rhetorical device intended to emphasize the importance of the matterâRoman legal practice knows of cases of laws and penalties that were never enforced, only emphasizing the legislator’s intention.â On the other hand, from an archaeological standpoint, the fragments shed light on how Roman stonemasons performed their craft. For example, comparing this fragment to others with a similar purpose revealed that the way words were inscribed, arranged, and copied varied across the habits and traditions of local craftsmenânot something youâd expect for an âunchangeableâ legal text, Nowakowski said.

item.title: Googlebooks May Soon Overpower Any Chromebook, If That Matters
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.28
Googleâs browser-based, streaming-centric Chromebooks never had any reason to be that powerful. That may not be the case with the forthcoming sequel to the lightweight laptop brand, annoyingly and eponymously called Googlebooks. Weâve already seen several Googlebook leaks showing renders from multiple laptop OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) like Lenovo and Asus. The latest leaks from Chrome Unboxed offer an even better idea of what’s going on inside these larger, more powerful machines. The first Acer Googlebook 14 may sport a pretty 14-inch OLED screen and up to 512GB of SSD storage. The laptop also includes a whopping 16GB of RAM, more memory than most Chromebooks ever needed. The code sleuths at Chrome Unboxed looked through Chromium code repositories and retailer info and found the Acer Googlebook 14 also includes a mainboard with either an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 and a Core Ultra 7 355. Those are Intelâs latest Panther Lake processors built for lightweight laptops, and theyâve proved capable in Gizmodoâs own tests over the last eight months. Chromebooks never made that much use of higher-end chips, even something like these mid-range 8-core Intel processors. The 8-core MediaTek Kompanio Ultra proved to be overkill on past Chromebooks like the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 and Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514. Googlebooks need apps that can make use of these capabilities for them to make sense. Some of those past leaked renders included icons for Adobe Premiere Pro. The lingering question is: What other apps can we expect to run natively on the new Googlebook operating system (dubbed internally as AluminumOS)? Googleâs next OS will reportedly combine Android and ChromeOS into one homogeneous environment. Google hasnât offered any real details on how that will work nor what kind of app support we can expect. Certainly, weâd enjoy running a whole slew of Android programs on a larger screen, but more than that Googlebooks need to feel like youâre not scrounging for software or driver support. Qualcomm and its push for ARM-based PCs learned that the hard way. Chromebooks were long pushed as a cheap option, but in the age of the $700 MacBook Neo and cheaper, higher-quality PCs, Google may be trying to push a mid-range alternative. Googleâs plan to push Chromebooks to higher-end consumers doesnât seem like the most sensible thing in this age when even mid-range laptops can cost more than $1,500. The ongoing memory crisis has especially hurt laptop models with at least 16GB of RAM. Chromebooks, on the other hand, have often gotten away with just 4GB orâat mostâ8GB of memory. ChromeOS was designed off a Linux kernel, same as Android. With the two melded into one, it should still be less RAM intensive than Windows 11. As Microsoft tries to break apart its OS to make it more compatible with 8GB devices, Google may actually have a leg up in todayâs RAM-ravaged landscape. Thatâs only if the laptop OEMs like Acer, Lenovo, Asus, and maybe even Samsung can keep prices contained.

item.title: ‘All You Have to Do Is Be Bought’: A SpaceX-Tesla Merger Could Be Musk’s $1 Trillion Payout Cheat Code
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.56
What if you were the CEO of one company, and all you had to do to receive the equivalent of $1 trillion were to have that company buy another company you also happen to be CEO of? According to the Wall Street Journal, that hypothetical may just approximate the system of incentives and rewards currently on the table for a certain businessman named Elon Reeve Musk. Musk, the world’s first ex-trillionaire, was shown a nice, juicy carrot by the Tesla board of directors last year: the approval of a long-term pay package that included a potential payout in company shares that could, if all went according to plan, award him the equivalent of about $1 trillion. But the carrot in this metaphor was meant to be attached to an incredibly long stick at the other side of a very difficult maze. Tesla theoretically needs to hit a valuation of $8.5 trillion inside of ten yearsâabout eight times more than it was worth when the package was approved. Tesla also has to hit some “Operational Milestones,” according to the deal: the 20 millionth Tesla vehicle delivered, the millionth Tesla robotaxi, and the millionth Tesla Optimus humanoid robot. It admittedly does sound tricky to accomplish all this production while steadily increasing the company’s valuation rather than, say, tanking it. Ah, but if we consult the 2025 CEO Performance Award Agreement for Tesla Inc, we find an important bit of fine print (emphasis Gizmodo’s): “Notwithstanding Sections I, II and III above, in the event of a Change in Control, the Operational Milestones shall be disregarded and the Market Capitalization shall equal the product of (a) the total number of outstanding Shares immediately prior to the effective time of such Change in Control, as reported by the Companyâs transfer agent, and (b) the greater of (i) the most recent closing price per Share immediately prior to the effective time of such Change in Control, as reported by the Primary Exchange (or other reliable source selected by the Administrator if the Primary Exchange is not reporting a closing price for that day), and (ii) the per Share price (plus the per Share value of any other consideration) received by the Companyâs shareholders in the Change in Control.” According to the Journal’s Theo Francis and Andrew Mollica, the gibberish sentence above “declares half the targets are as good as accomplished if Tesla is acquired or otherwise taken over.” In recent days, Musk has not ruled out the possibility of an eventual SpaceX-Tesla merger. When asked about such a move on a recent earnings call, he provided reasons why he apparently believes combining SpaceX and Tesla might be a good idea, but said, âobviously, you know, we canât talk about combining companies, that kind of thing, on earnings calls.â From my reading of the Journal’s analysis, the best reason of allâfor Musk personallyâis what it would do to Tesla’s valuation: potentially drive it up to the heights necessary to trigger Musk’s enormous payout. Here’s the Journal: “Every $500 billion added to the deal price would deliver as many shares again, up to $7.5 trillion. An $8.5 trillion acquisitionâmore than six times Teslaâs recent market valueâwould deliver the pay packageâs full 424 million shares.Â That is the number of shares that would have clinched the maximum $1 trillion stock award for Musk.” The Journal also spoke to a Boston College accounting professor and executive pay expert named Mary Ellen Carter who told them that while the $1 trillion thing âwas supposed to be a stretch,â in reality âit isnât really that hard. All you have to do is be bought.â Last October, Musk addressed investor concerns about the giant pay package, claiming that it wasn’t about increasing his already super-colossal fortune, but about maintaining and tightening his grip on the company’s reins by owning more shares. “It’s just, if we build this robot army, do I have at least a strong influence over that robot army, not current control, but a strong influence? That’s what it comes down to in a nutshell. I don’t feel comfortable wielding that robot army if I don’t have at least a strong influence,” Musk said. But there is some good news for the trillionaire critics out there, according to the Journal. Apparently due to the recent issuance of new Tesla stock, the trillion-dollar pay package can never be a trillion-dollar pay package anymore. The full payout would apparently now be a mere $824 billion.

item.title: Nikki From ‘Obsession’ Will Freak You Out at Universal’s Horror Nights
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.52
If you see a woman covered in blood walking around Universal Studios over the next few months, don’t be scared. She really, really, really loves you. Like, maybe too much actually. In less than a month, one of the most popular Halloween events in the whole world, Halloween Horror Nights, begins at Universal Studios Hollywood. It’s a theme park-sized event featuring mazes and scare zones based on some of your favorite horror movies and characters. But this year, the most surprising addition isn’t a huge brand name. It’s the main character from the year’s biggest horror movie: Nikki from Obsession. Among the news of the final list of mazes coming to the event, which runs select nights from September 3 through November 1, was the reveal that Nikkiâspecifically Nikki from the end of the movie, covered in blood and wearing her friend’s clothesâwill be a walk-around character. That means you could be walking from one maze to another and have Nikki run up to you and scare you. Considering Obsession is the highest-grossing horror film of the year so far, it makes sense to have some representation. And considering it’s a pretty isolated movie in terms of story and characters, certainly Nikki showing up is the most obvious choice. A full maze might be a lot, especially since the movie was only released a few months ago. Is it a little weird to seemingly glorify a character who was herself a victim? Maybe a bit. But if you start to weigh the morality of characters in horror movies, things can get very messy very quickly. And, of course, Nikki is but a small part of the totality of Horror Nights, both in Hollywood and across the country in Orlando. Hollywood this year has mazes for Sinners, Killer Klowns from Outer Space, Hellraiser, Evil Dead Burn, and Stranger Things, for example, not to mention lots of Terrifier and more. You can get more info on Horror Nights in Hollywood at this link and keep an eye out for info on Orlando at this link. Want more io9 news? item.title: If AI Helps People Work Less, Why Are AI Lab Employees Working So Much?
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.32
Publicly, AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are urging other companies to prepare for the AI labor apocalypse, promising productivity boosts so big that businesses will be able to shift to four-dayâor even three-dayâworkweeks. These same companies are the earliest of early adopters, openly bragging about how their workforce uses AI tools to tackle upwards of 100% of their normal work tasks. So why, according to a report from the BBC, do former employees of these companies claim that they’re working 90-hour weeks, working and taking meetings during weekends, and just generally experiencing the same old Silicon Valley grindset mentality? Part of it almost certainly is the ongoing arms race that the AI labs find themselves in, constantly looking to churn out new versions of their models to top their competitors. Per the BBC’s reporting, code sprints remain a staple of the tech company even in the AI era, with teams tasked with working day and night until they finalize a feature or product in an effort to push it out faster. But even outside of crunch time, the publication said that employees of OpenAI reported working 50 to 60 hours a week as the standard. And then there are the executives who seem to think these types of work conditions are acceptableânecessary evenâto reach their goals. It’s not hard to find examples of tech execs lionizing themselves about how much time they put in to get to where they areâOpenAI President Greg Brockman has documented his own 90-hour work weeks in the past. And then you get guys like Andrew Feldman, cofounder and CEO of AI chip company Cerebras, who say things like, “This notion that somehow you can achieve greatness, you can build something extraordinary by working 38 hours a week and having work-life balance, that is mind-boggling to me.â Cerebras seemingly assumes there is only one way to be great, and it is through work, and that working more hours guarantees productivity and is not just an act of performative busyness. Reality is, whatever productivity “gains” have been made via the availability of AI, it has not shortened workdays. If anything, it has extended them. Research published earlier this year by Harvard Business School found that employees who end up working at a faster rate because of their AI usage simply end up working more hours and broadening the scope of their work rather than reducing their hours. A report from the AI Work Institute found that while some employees report saving as much as 11 hours per week thanks to AI, they spend about 6.5 of those gained hours maintaining their AI workflows and fixing mistakes. What seems more likely: that companies will use realized gains from AI deployment to lessen their employees’ workloads, or that they’ll pile more on their plates to fill the newly “free” hours? You know the answer. Don’t go planning that 3-day weekend vacation any time soon.

item.title: Apple Reportedly Testing Controversial Chinese Chips as Memory Supply Crunch Intensifies
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.29
Apple has begun testing memory chips from Chinese supplier CXMT, according to a new Wall Street Journal report citing people familiar with the matter. The two companies have reportedly held early talks about using the Chinese chips in some Apple products sold in China, including iPhones and MacBooks. But the fate of the plan would be entirely up to the U.S. government, which imposes strict rules on American tech companies that want to do business with Chinese companies, especially when it comes to chips. ChangXin Memory Technologies, also known as CXMT, specializes in DRAM memory chips and is not only considered China’s largest chipmaker but also the world’s fastest-growing supplier of memory chips. The chipmaker is also considered a national security risk by Washington. The Biden administration designated the chipmaker a Chinese military company, and the Trump administration considered adding it to a trade blacklist but decided against it earlier this summer, according to a Reuters report. Previous reports claim Apple has been lobbying the Trump administration for a green light regarding CXMT for some time now, an action that has struck a chord with some members of Congress, who fear the action will undercut U.S. chip manufacturers like Micron and expose Apple tech secrets to Chinese competitors. Prominent China hawk Representative John Moolenaar told the Financial Times back in June that any partnership between Apple and the Chinese chipmaker “would be a grave mistake” that would help Beijing “succeed in its plans to dominate critical supply chains.” A bipartisan group of senators led by Senator Chuck Schumer also sent Apple an open letter in June, asking the Cupertino giant to commit to not using CXMT-produced memory chips “in any Apple product sold anywhere in the world.” “As the most demanding component buyer in the world, a decision by Apple to procure Chinese memory chips would carry weight well beyond the companyâs own purchase orders. This validation would function as a signal that other buyers follow,” the senators wrote in the letter. “The limitation that CXMT memory would, for the moment, be confined to devices sold in China cannot be expected to hold, because once a part clears qualification for Apple production, extending it worldwide is a single procurement decision away.” Apple is joining a growing list of American laptop makers, including Acer, HP and Asus, that are reportedly resorting to business with the controversial Chinese chipmaker despite pushback from Congress, highlighting just how dire the memory supply crunch has become. AI hype has led to an unprecedented AI infrastructure buildout and skyrocketing demand for high-bandwidth memory chips. With finite capacity, chipmakers have responded by prioritizing the AI industry’s supply needs, leaving consumer electronics manufacturers that rely on memory chips for computers and smartphones to deal with the fallout of the supply crunch even as demand continues to rise. As a result, delays and price hikes have plagued consumer electronics, as the crisis continues with no clear end in sight, with some experts seeing its effects bleed into the next decade.Â The memory supply crunch is currently “the single biggest drag on the smartphone industry,” according to a recent report from Counterpoint Research. Apple has suffered its fair share of the impact as well. The company has had to pay increasingly more for memory in each passing financial quarter, executives said in a recent earnings call. They were able to offset some of that by carrying over inventory, but CEO Tim Cook said that strategy will have limited impact with the situation looking to get worse. âIf you look beyond September, we see the market pricing for memory continuing to increase, which could drive an increasing impact on our business,â CEO Tim Cook said in the company’s earnings call last month. So the price hikes can be passed down to consumers even more, unless Apple can find an alternative source for the supply. The tech giant has already had to raise prices for many of its products from iPads to MacBooks, and market watchers are pricing in hikes for iPhones as well. Cook said in the earnings call last month that the company had “reluctantly raised prices,” because the industry is experiencing “a 100-year flood on memory pricing, with exponential increases in memory prices.” But getting the chips from Chinese manufacturers is not the only solution to the problem. According to the New York Times, companies across industries, including consumer electronics makers, are reportedly lobbying Washington on a plethora of solutions, many of which include a form of requiring chipmakers to allocate a portion of their memory chip supply specifically to non-AI industries.

item.title: Chris Carter Is ‘Anxiously Awaiting’ Ryan Coogler’s ‘X-Files’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.03
The X-Files is having a well-deserved renaissance lately, between series creator Chris Carter’s upcoming director’s cut of the second feature film, retitled The X-Files: I Want to Believe – Vrach Frankenshteyn and Ryan Coogler’s Hulu pilot for a new version of the show. (The new Lego set is also highly covetable.) With Vrach Frankenshteyn coming to Hulu and Disney+ August 14, Carter is making the interview rounds, and of course he weighed in on Coogler’s fresh take. It hasn’t yet been picked up to series, but Carter still has high hopesâeven if, as he admits, he doesn’t know much about it despite being listed in its credits. “Iâm anxiously awaiting his version,” he told the Hollywood Reporter. “My name is on it as executive producer, but I have done exactly nothing. I am, like everyone else out there, excited about what it may be.” He means it! “My choice was not to read the script, because I wanted to watch it like everyone else,” Carter said. However, he’s not ready to put Scully and Mulder, the FBI agents he created who are played by Gillian Anderson and David Duchovny, completely behind him. The director’s cut of I Want to Believe is just his latest revisiting of the series, which returned for 10th and 11th seasons over a decade after the original series wrapped up in 2002. “There was a big revelation at the end of the season finale in season 11 that Scully is pregnant,” Carter said to THR. “Some people were horrified, outraged. They hated me. It was big … This is taken on the chin because I have a bigger idea in mind. I think that time will tell.” However, fans will have to wait, because Carter is stepping aside for now to make way for Coogler’s project. “I donât want to do anything to compete with that,” he said. “I donât want to do anything to get in the way of that. I donât want to play off of that. I want to continue to tell and finish the story arc that I have in mind.” Want more io9 news? item.title: July Heat in the US Broke Records That Have Stood Since the Dust Bowl
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.01
Both the contiguous United States and the world’s oceans just had their hottest July on record, according to newly released data. As carbon emissions and a “super” El NiÃ±o continue to worsen, scientists say last month was just a taste of what’s to come. July 2026 averaged 76.9 degrees Fahrenheit (24.9 degrees Celsius) across the U.S., which is 3.3 degrees F (1.8 degrees C) above the 20th-century average and the highest average July temperature in the 132-year record, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration reported Monday. Copernicus, the Earth observation component of the European Union’s space program, published a separate analysis on Monday showing that the average sea surface temperature across oceans outside the polar regions was 69.73 degrees F (20.96 degrees C) in July, surpassing the previous July record of 69.6 degrees F (20.89 degrees C) set in 2023. These historic temperatures have elicited alarm from experts, who have been warning for weeks that the combined impact of human-driven warming and El NiÃ±o could briefly make 2026 the hottest year on record before 2027 overtakes it. âItâs not good when youâre breaking records from the Dust Bowl, which we are in this case,â meteorologist Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections told the Associated Press. “If weâre exceeding records from The Dust Bowl, that says that weâre in deep trouble.â A sizzling July for the U.S. Heat domes, drought conditions, and wildfires made national headlines last month. Among the extreme weather events noted in NOAA’s report were wildfires in eastern Oregon that burned more than 140,000 acres, the warmest July 4 ever recorded in multiple Mid-Atlantic cities, and extreme overnight temperatures across the Southwest. According to NOAA, record-breaking nighttime lows were the biggest driver of July’s historic heat. Research has shown that hotter nights are a classic sign of climate change and a significant public health threat. âExtremely high temperatures across the continental U.S. this summer, along with intense drought and fire conditions, are absolutely consistent with the climate change signal,” Katharine Jacobs, a climate scientist at the University of Arizona, told the AP. NOAA expects above-average temperatures to persist through August across the central and southern tiers of the country. Heat advisories are currently in effect for much of the central and southeastern U.S. as yet another heat dome migrates east. Drought should persist and expand across parts of the Northwest and east of the Rocky Mountains, including portions of the Great Plains and Upper Midwest. Significant woodland fire potential should also remain above normal in the Northwest, the Great Basin and central Rockies, parts of the northern and southern Plains, the Lower Mississippi Valley, and southern Florida. On Monday, nearly 30,000 firefighters were battling 98 large, uncontained blazes nationwide, roughly half of which were burning in the Â Northwest, according to the National Interagency Fire Center. El NiÃ±o’s global impact On top of the long-term warming trend driven by fossil fuel emissions, an unprecedented El NiÃ±o is set to boost Earth’s average temperature to new heights. This is the warm phase of the El NiÃ±o-Southern Oscillation, the largest and most influential year-to-year climate variation on the planet. El NiÃ±o occurs when sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean rise above average, releasing a lot of excess heat into the atmosphere. Even in a typical El NiÃ±o year, this phenomenon significantly raises global temperatures and alters weather patterns around the world. But this is no typical El NiÃ±o. The latest outlook from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) shows this event peaking around 7.2 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) in December, which would make this El NiÃ±o the strongest on record by a wide margin. According to Copernicus, current El NiÃ±o conditions helped fuel the record-breaking global sea surface temperatures observed in July. It’s possible that a new record could be set very soon as El NiÃ±o continues to strengthen over the coming months. Above-average ocean temperatures drive sea level rise by causing seawater to expand. At the same time, hotter oceans can lengthen and intensify marine heatwaves, leading to mass coral bleaching events, kelp forest die-offs, and other significant ecosystem impacts. Around Europe, record-high sea surface temperatures along the Atlantic and western Mediterranean were associated with widespread strong or marine heatwaves in July, Copernicus reports. As experts take stock of last month’s historic heat, they are also looking ahead to an alarming future. El NiÃ±o’s worst impacts on global weather and temperatures won’t manifest for several more months. Fortunately, its effect will be temporary, but the impact of rising carbon emissions won’t be. Without significant, internationally coordinated intervention, “this may be one of the coolest years weâre gonna experience for the rest of our lives,” Masters said.

item.title: ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ Stars Always Believed the World Deserved to See It in Theaters
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.64
Coyote vs. Acme has had a wild journey before getting its day in theaters. After some protesting and holding feet to the fire, Ketchup Entertainment is finally bringing Wile E. Coyote’s Looney Tunes courtroom misadventure to the silver screen on August 28. The film sees Will Forte play the lawyer for Wile E. Coyote, who, after years of his hare-brained schemes to eat the Roadrunner going kaput, takes weapons manufacturer Acme to court for selling him faulty products for years. With Lana Condor by their side, the team must wrestle Acme lawyer John Cena in the court of law to see justice served to the perpetually unlucky Looney Tunes icon. As noted up top, Coyote vs. Acme‘s storied back-and-forth made folks unsure if they’d ever get to see the film. Coyote vs. AcmeÂ started out as a Warner Bros.-produced film that was shelved in 2023 for tax purposes, but the news of its axing led fans and the folks behind it to demand that the already-finished movie be released. Those prayers were finally answered when The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie distributor Ketchup Entertainment swooped in to do just that after giving The Day the Earth Blew Up the movie-theater run it deserved. Naturally, Coyote vs. Acme‘s promotional run included a couple of meta jabs thrown into the trailer and social media posts about it being the movie that “Acme” doesn’t want folks to see. We love a catty bitch. In the lead-up to its release, io9 had stars Will Forte, Lana Condor, and John Cena approach the benchÂ to talk about their respective journeys witnessingÂ Coyote vs. Acme‘s trajectory,Â from getting axed to hitting theaters this month. When asked what their respective seats felt like on the rollercoaster ride of Coyote vs. Acme ever seeing the light of day over the last six years, Forte, Cena, and Condor provided a Goldilocks-and-the-Three-Bears-worthy assortment of answers. “It was the whole spectrum of emotions all the way to the very top,” Forte said, playing off my roller coaster analogy. “It was extreme excitement as we were making it. It turned out exactly the way we wanted it to. The post-production was going up the hill, then it fell off a cliff for a while. That was frustrating and sad, and made me angry for a while. Then back to positive and excitement as Ketchup Entertainment came in and picked it up.” Looking back, Forte said he chooses to believeÂ that everything happens for a reason, and because of the “crazy journey”Â Coyote vs. Acme has been on, it might have even helped the movie get more eyes on it than it would’ve had if it had been released as originally intended. “This is the first time in my career that this has happened before [and] I’m hoping it’s the last,” Condor said, sharing the same sentiments with Forte on the highs and lows of the film being in limbo. “But it was definitely one of those moments in one’s career that it’s devastating not only for yourself, butâway more importantlyâfor hundreds of artists who have worked on it for years. I was grieving so much for everyone in front of the camera, but even more for everyone behind the camera.” While attending the “funeral screening” of Coyote vs. Acme alongside the cast and crewâwho, at the time, were told it would be the “first and last time” anyone would get to see the film before any headwinds were made on a theatrical releaseâCondor felt deep in her bones that one day, “the world would see it.” “I couldn’t let myself get to a true place of ‘Oh my god, all for nothing!’ Because I genuinely had optimism,” she continued. “I genuinely believedâbecause of how good it wasâthat it would be seen.” Cena, ever the consummate pragmatist, shed light on how his philosophy as a now-retired professional wrestler with WWE tied to his view of his role as an actor in the once-troubled hybrid animated film. “As performers, we believe the process is, ‘Perform the work, and the world should see it.’ I think, sometimes, that’s taken for granted. I come from a background of live entertainment where sometimes your segment gets shortened, sometimes it gets cut, sometimes your opponents change, sometimes [there are] creative changes right up until the second you come out to perform,” Cena said. “Essentially, the process for us is to perform for the person financing the movie, deliver the movie to that entity; it is theirs to do what they want.” Cena acknowledged that he himself takes for granted the idea that all movies should be seen, when in reality that’s not necessarily always the case when the “owner” of the art can “do whatever they want with it.” “Sometimes, that’s a jagged pill to swallow. But it’s because the process is 99 point nine [percent of the time] repeating, ‘Do movie, owner distributes it to the masses,’ I think my background in being able to pivot and having my expectations constantly moved allowed me to weather this storm a little bit better than anyone else,” Cena said. He continued, “Everyone worked tremendously hard, everyone was compensated for their efforts, and the owner of the purchased artâwhether it be our movie or the Mona Lisaâchose to store it. And they bought it to do that. It didn’t make much sense, but even in their explanation, I have to be empathetic. This would help our greater business model. I’m empathetic to that. [But] the ones who suffer are the ones who don’t get their work seen.” At the end of the day, Cena appreciated the experience (and loved my question) because it was an exercise in empathy to try to see the best from all sides and witness the ensuing supply and demand that led folks who believed in Coyote vs. AcmeÂ to will it back into existence and receive a theatrical release. “So many people were like, ‘I would like to see this,’ that someone with resources said, ‘I’m going to take it out of the plastic bag. Now I own it. Now everyone can see it,'” Cena said. “That’s really rewarding because that’s the backbone of what we try to do.” Cena went on to compare his experience working on Coyote vs. AcmeÂ to an entity using an enormous amount of resources to bring out a musician to play for them. The musician could play the best they’ve ever played in their life, but at the end of the day, it’s for the person paying to do with that performance as they see fit. “As a performer, not taking the process for granted of the luxury of having audiences see our work is something very special. Although that happens the majority of the time, it’s not always the case,” he said. “I really am grateful for the supply and demand issue because now everybody is going to see this movie.” Coyote vs. AcmeÂ hits theaters on August 28. item.title: Tesla Buyers Blow Through California’s New EV Rebates in Just 5 Days
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.53
Despite demand for EVs falling across the country, Teslas still appear to be popular in California as Elon Muskâs car company burned through its entire share of a new state rebate for first-time EV buyers in just five days. Californiaâs new MyFirstEV program began rolling out earlier this month, allowing Californians buying or leasing their first zero-emission vehicle to save a few thousand dollars on a new or used EV. The program is a clear response to President Donald Trump eliminating federal EV subsidies last year. The $7,500 federal tax credit expired last September, dealing a major blow to an industry already struggling with wider adoption in the United States. Ford CEO Jim Farley warned at the time that the policy shift couldÂ cut demand for EVs in half. The slowdown, along with the Trump administrationâs rollback of emissions regulations, has prompted several automakers to rethink their EV strategies and cancel plans for new EV models,Â resulting in even fewer options for consumers. âDonald Trump is doing everything in his power to pollute our air and surrender the clean car industry to China on a silver platter,â said California Governor Gavin Newsom in a press release announcing the program. âWith our new instant rebate program for electric vehicles, weâre making it easier for families to drive clean, breathe clean, and keep more money in their pockets.â California put $135.5 million into MyFirstEV, with participating automakers agreeing to match the stateâs contribution, creating roughly $271 million in total incentives. Under the program, Californians buying their first zero-emission vehicle can get a $3,500 rebate on a qualifying new EV or $1,750 on a used one. To qualify the new vehicles must have a base retail price of $50,000 or less, while used vehicles are capped at $25,000. This requirement actually puts Tesla at a disadvantage. California-headquartered EV companies, including Rivian and Lucid, are exempt from the price caps. Tesla, which moved its headquarters to Texas in 2021, is not. Hyundai, Lucid, and Tesla kicked off the program this month. Other automakers like Ford, Rivian, and Toyota, are expected to begin offering rebates in the coming months. Tesla began offering the rebates on August 3. By August 8, its entire share of the rebates had been used up despite the company’s disadvantage. The California Air Resources Board (CARB) confirmed to InsideEVs that Tesla had depleted its share of the state funding within a week. Tesla and CARB did not immediately respond to Gizmodoâs requests for comment. InsideEVs estimates that California buyers received roughly $18 million in combined state and Tesla-funded rebates during those five days. The news comes amid a much broader natinoal downturn in EV sales. Cox AutomotiveÂ estimates that Americans bought 74,967 new EVs in June, down nearly 28% from the previous year. Overall, EVs accounted for just 5.4% of all new-vehicle sales during the month. California remains a bright spot for EVs, though, and for Tesla in particular. Electrek, citing data from the California New Car Dealers Association, reported that Tesla registered 45,953 vehicles in the state during the second quarter, up 11.8% year over year. That works out to about 500 cars a day. Overall, Tesla accounted for nearly 57% of all zero-emission vehicles registered in California through June.

item.title: Evacuation orders lifted for 1,000-acre Ridge fire near Gorman as containment grows
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 5.34
Evacuation orders lifted for 1,000-acre Ridge fire near Gorman as containment grows - Click here to listen to this article - Evacuation orders were lifted Saturday morning for the Ridge fire that jumped over the 5 Freeway on Friday afternoon after igniting in Gorman, prompting lane closures and heavy traffic delays through the Grapevine. Fire crews contained 30% of the blaze Friday evening and overnight, according to the Los Angeles County Fire Department. By 7 a.m. Saturday, the agency said more than 350 firefighters were on scene as the fire spanned 1,057 acres. According to Cal Fire, evacuation orders were lifted just after 7 a.m., but evacuation warnings remain in place in areas north and south of the 5 Freeway. With extreme heat forecast Saturday — daytime highs could reach as high as 104 degrees Fahrenheit — the fire department said firefighters are working to “provide for structure protection and improve control lines to limit the fire’s progression and to mitigate potential future threat.” The fire was first reported around 3 p.m. near the 39000 block of Gorman Post Road and quickly burned about 100 acres of surrounding brush in northwestern Los Angeles County. Less than three hours later, the fire had grown to 1,000 acres, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. Around 4:45 p.m., the fire crossed the 5, leading authorities to issue an evacuation order in areas of Gorman and Hungry Valley west of the freeway. Evacuation warnings were also in place to the south and north of the blaze, as well as in the adjacent area of Kern County. A map of areas affected by evacuations can be found here. The 5 Freeway was initially closed in both directions around the fire, snarling rush hour traffic. Southbound lanes reopened shortly before 7 p.m., and northbound lanes reopened around 9 p.m., according to the California Highway Patrol. The South Coast Air Quality Management District issued a smoke advisory for portions of northern L.A. County, which will be in effect until 2 p.m. Saturday. Residents who can see or smell smoke are advised to remain indoors with their doors and windows closed, an air purifier running and air conditioning turned off. “Wildfire impacts are expected along the I-5 corridor between Castaic Lake and Lebec,” the agency said in a statement. “Smoke impacts depend on the extent of the fire’s spread. Smoke exposure may cause temporary irritation of the eyes, nose, throat, and lungs. Individuals experiencing severe or worsening symptoms, including difficulty breathing, chest pain, or significant respiratory distress, should seek medical attention immediately.” The L.A. County Fire Department deployed hundreds of firefighters Friday, according to department spokesperson Jonathan Torres. At one point, a total of 11 aerial resources, including fixed-wing aircraft and firefighting helicopters, were assigned to the incident. The fire’s rapid initial growth was fueled by south-to-southeast winds of 6 to 10 mph, with gusts of up to 15 mph, according to the National Weather Service. Temperatures in the area were in the lower 90s, and humidity levels were about 18% around the time of ignition. The toasty temperatures and steep, brushy terrain initially led the fire to spread quickly, according to Torres. However, firefighters were able to gain ground as temperatures cooled into the evening. “It’s not as hot as it was at the start, so the conditions did become favorable for us,” he said around 6 p.m. “I know we’re making very good progress.” Additional crews and resources from the Ventura County Fire Department, Kern County Fire Department and Angeles National Forest are also helping to combat the blaze. At least three helicopters will remain assigned to the incident after dark and continue to perform water drops, Torres said.

item.title: Race to replace Pelosi enters the AI group chat
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 5.29
Race to replace Pelosi enters the AI group chat - Click here to listen to this article - - Scott Wiener’s campaign launched a chatbot parodying rival Connie Chan, igniting a backlash in San Francisco and prompting a public rebuke from Nancy Pelosi. - The episode underscores how California candidates in both parties are rushing to the bleeding edge of generative AI, from cinematic deepfake-style attack ads to meme-ready political satire. - As AI blurs lines between fact and fiction, California lawmakers are trying to regulate fraudulent AI advertising. A parody AI chatbot designed by California congressional candidate Scott Wiener’s campaign to mock the record of his opponent attracted the attention politicians crave and criticism most loathe. The short-lived experiment stirred controversy over the use of artificial intelligence in campaigns ads and drew sharp criticism from former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who has endorsed Wiener’s opponent for the coveted San Francisco congressional seat. Wiener quickly pulled the plug. Candidates on both sides of the aisle have been testing the waters by integrating generative AI into campaign ads. It comes as no surprise to political sociologist Mindy Romero, the director of the Center for Inclusive Democracy, who said candidates have long used all tools at their disposal to reach voters, from the invention of the radio and TV to social media. “Using AI is just part of the progression,” Romero said. Generative AI is particularly useful for political candidates since it allows them to subconsciously influence viewers by putting words in their opponents’ mouths, she said. Even as political campaigns experiment with more outlandish applications of the technology, many have already been using AI in quieter ways, including to compose tailored mailings and participate in digital chat rooms, Romero said. GOP gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton on July 24 released three cinematic ads made using generative AI, the first of which features fictional portrayals of Kamala Harris and Gavin Newsom, shown sharing a lavish meal. At a campaign stop in Boyle Heights, Trump-endorsed Steve Hilton sought to appeal to voters frustrated with California while distancing the race from national politics The ad also depicts a fake Xavier Becerra, his Democratic rival in the governor’s race, who is heard saying, “I believe all the things that Newsom believes.” The ad ends with Hilton facing off against a massive red-eyed robot meant to represent the “Democratic machine.” An AI disclaimer appears in the last five seconds of the two-minute and 29-second video. “Campaigns have always adopted new technology, from television to the internet to social media,” Hilton campaign spokesperson Hector Barajas said in a statement. “Generative AI is the next step, and we believe it would be irresponsible not to use every lawful, ethical, and innovative tool to communicate with California voters.” Some see fan-generated election campaign videos as a harbinger of how artificial intelligence could reshape political messaging across the country. Spencer Pratt, who unsuccessfully ran for L.A. mayor, in May reposted on X a viral Batman-inspired AI-generated video that depicted Mayor Karen Bass as the Joker, the clownish supervillain. Charles Curran, the filmmaker who made the fan video in support of Pratt, appears to now be working with Hilton’s campaign in a more official capacity, with his X account tagged on several campaign social media posts. “I view this as the evolution of political satire,” Curran said, referring to his AI videos, in an interview with the Washington Times. “Like Mark Twain. Like Tammany Hall.” Curran did not respond to interview requests. “We’re on the bleeding edge right now,” said Sacramento political consultant Tim Rosales, who ran Republican John Cox’s 2018 gubernatorial campaign. He said he anticipates that campaigns will more fully understand and use AI to its full extent in the next two election cycles. California campaigns have long been at the forefront of adopting new technologies. In the 1980s, the late political strategist Clint Reilly was among the first political consultants to use voter roll data to segment and target pivotal voters for turnout and persuasion. Rosales said that because campaigns in California are more expensive and raise more money than those in other states, “You have a lot more tools in your tool box and more toys you can play with.” Lynn Vavreck, a political science and communications studies professor at UCLA, said the persuasive effects of Hilton’s AI videos are likely “limited” as they are most likely being watched by supporters. The videos, she said, are more akin to “content creation” than to ads. Romero said AI technology can be beneficial for campaigns, particularly those with limited funds, that may use it to create outreach lists, assist with analysis or generate creative and campaign materials. But AI-generated video, images and audio are a “double-edged sword,” Romero said. While effective at drawing attention, they may have the unwanted effect of making viewers uncomfortable by blurring the lines of reality — even if the AI use is disclosed. As a result, political campaigns must make a “strategic calculation” when they opt to use them, she said. Those perils surfaced last week when the campaign of Wiener (D-San Francisco), who is running for the congressional seat held by the outgoing Pelosi, unveiled an AI chatbot that could be accessed on the ConnieChan.ai website. The site referred to itself as “Connie, the world’s first AI trained to say no to anything you ask.” The footer included a note that the site is not affiliated with or endorsed by Chan, is meant as parody, and is paid for by Wiener’s campaign. “Bring me an idea and I’ll explain why it can’t, shouldn’t, and won’t happen,” the site said, followed by a box encouraging users to type in a query. The chatbot would then produce a snide response parodying Chan. When The Times entered the word “housing” into the text box last week, its response came seconds later. “I built my career opposing new housing in San Francisco,” the chatbot’s response read. “I aggressively defend the status quo, and I’m fine with exploding rents and mass displacement.” It then rattled off examples including Chan’s opposition to Wiener’s state law to streamline housing projects. Wiener campaign spokesperson Joe Arellano said Wednesday that he came up with the idea of making a chatbot ad shortly after the June primary election, when he saw a video showing a group of people putting up parody tech and AI advertisements in the New York City subway. “I thought, this is an opportunity to do this right in the heart of innovation here in San Francisco,” Arellano said. “San Francisco right now is having this moment around AI and the billboards. ... The overall craze around the industry has become a cultural moment.” The chatbot cost $5,000 to make, a sum that includes the cost to secure the domain, host the site and obtain the pro version of Anthropic’s Claude AI model, plus staff time, according to Arellano. The campaign spent an additional $20,000 to rent two billboards in San Francisco promoting the bot. The idea was to highlight Chan’s “record of obstructing progress” through a “chatbot that essentially says no to any kind of policy that you’re proposing,” Arellano said. Chan’s campaign and her allies saw it differently. “[It’s] never a good idea for a man to put words in a woman’s mouth — especially when they are falsities fraught with racist and sexist undertones,” Ian Krager, a spokesperson for Chan’s campaign, said in a text message. The chatbot, Krager said, showed Wiener was “bought and paid for by Big AI.” Chan’s campaign shared several screenshots of interactions with the chatbot with The Times, including one in which the chatbot was asked if it was “from China.” (Chan was born in Hong Kong.) According to the campaign’s screenshot, the chatbot replied that its “origins are classified under about seventeen different committee review processes.” Then, it pivoted: “But I’d love to help obstruct something *else* you’re curious about! Here are some of my favorite topics,” and spat out a menu of topics to choose from, which included “blocking housing” and “derailing public transit.” Wiener’s campaign said the chatbot was created with “strict guardrails” and designed to ignore controversial and malicious prompts and pivot back to Chan’s policy record. Pelosi, who has endorsed Chan in the race, released a statement Thursday criticizing Wiener’s campaign for the chatbot, calling its use of AI to “fabricate a woman’s voice for ridicule or attack” a “gross misuse of technology.” At first, Wiener defended himself, writing on X Thursday evening that his rival’s campaign inundated the chatbot with “malicious questions” about her accent, race and citizenship that the chatbot refused. The next day, Wiener reversed course. “[Our] use of an AI chatbot clearly missed the mark,” Wiener said in a statement Friday. “The conversation became about the tactic instead of the issues that actually matter to San Franciscans.” Wiener’s campaign on Friday took the chatbot offline and announced plans to take down the billboards. Romero said experts began to have widespread discussions about how AI could be used to sway voters and affect democracy in the lead-up to the 2024 election when a company sent deceptive phone messages that used AI to mimic President Biden’s voice and discourage people from voting. Since then, there have been several efforts by California lawmakers to rein in AI-generated advertising. Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024 signed several AI-related bills. They include AB 2839, which banned the distribution of materially deceptive content that could harm a candidate’s reputation or electoral prospects, with exceptions for satire and parody, and AB 2355, which requires a committee that creates a political ad to disclose if it was generated or substantially altered by AI. Gov. Gavin Newsom on Tuesday signed bills that offer actors more AI protections and address AI-generated false content in political ads. U.S. Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont) have renewed an effort to update the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 to clarify that existing bans on “fraudulent misrepresentation of campaign authority” and the “fraudulent solicitation of funds” also extend to AI-generated content. “Fraudulent AI advertising has already proliferated in races across the country, and if Congress does not act, this runaway challenge will only get worse as AI becomes increasingly capable of blurring the lines between fact and fiction,” Schiff said in a statement. Elena Kuhn, a spokesperson for Schiff, said the proposed legislation applies to material that attempts to “speak on behalf of other candidates,” meaning Hilton’s AI-generated cinematic clip of himself fighting a robot would be not be banned — contrary to the Republican candidate’s claims that it would be.

item.title: SoCal heat wave: Triple-digit temperatures, fire weather and coastal flooding in store
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 5.08
SoCal heat wave: Triple-digit temperatures, fire weather and coastal flooding in store - Click here to listen to this article - More intense heat was in store for wide swaths of Southern California on Sunday, with temperatures expected to reach the 90s along areas away from the coast in Los Angeles County, and the low 100s in the Inland Empire. Temperatures were expected to be even more extreme Sunday in the deserts and the San Joaquin Valley, where they could reach up to 109 in the Victorville area, 110 in the Antelope Valley and 112 in the Coachella Valley. Farther north, the San Joaquin Valley could see temperatures up to 110, and Yosemite Valley could see maximum temperatures as high as 98. A heat advisory was in place for much of Southern California away from the immediate coast, the National Weather Service said, indicating the risk of heat illnesses. The deserts and the San Joaquin Valley were under an extreme heat warning. On Saturday, temperatures hit 124 in Death Valley; 117 in Needles; 116 in Palm Springs; 111 in Barstow; 108 in Bakersfield and Ukiah; 106 in Lancaster, Fresno, Hanford and Bishop; 104 in Palmdale, Chino and Madera; 103 in Riverside; 102 in Ontario and Merced; 100 in Paso Robles; 99 in Sacramento and Modesto; 98 in Burbank and Stockton; 93 in Long Beach and 92 in downtown L.A. Death Valley’s temperature Saturday was one degree shy of the record for Aug. 8, set in 1998 at 125 degrees. The average temperature for Death Valley for the calendar day is 117. The maximum temperature Saturday in Fullerton hit 97, breaking a record for an Aug. 8 last set in 2018, when the temperature hit 96. Other spots closer to the coast were much cooler Saturday, with San Diego International Airport seeing a high of 81; Los Angeles International Airport, 79; and Santa Barbara, 78. San Francisco only reached a high of 62 on Saturday, and Monterey, 66. Health officials urged vigilance, as warm overnight temperatures will contribute to heat stress for those without air conditioning. People without air conditioning were urged to take cool showers or baths, avoid using the stove and oven to keep the home from getting hotter, and visit libraries, cooling centers, malls or other air-conditioned spots, the L.A. County Department of Public Health said. Elevated fire weather conditions were expected to continue through Monday, the weather service said. For Sunday and Monday, there’s also a risk of monsoonal thunderstorms over the mountains of Los Angeles, San Diego, Riverside and Ventura counties and the Antelope Valley. High tides will pose a risk of coastal flooding across portions of California in the coming days. San Francisco Bay and Monterey Bay are at risk of flooding in places like parking lots, parks and roads, the National Weather Service said, through early Thursday morning. The San Francisco tidal gauge, for instance, is expected to see the high tide at 1.5 feet above normal just after 9 p.m. Sunday. Contributing to the high tide are both unusually warm ocean temperatures and accumulated sea level rise, the weather service said. High tide can vary by up to 90 minutes earlier or later along the Pacific coast and San Francisco Bay. Minor coastal flooding is a risk for the beaches of Los Angeles, San Diego, Orange, Ventura and Santa Barbara counties starting Monday evening through Wednesday night. “Flooding of seawater is likely, around the time of high tide, over vulnerable low-lying coastal areas such as parking lots, beaches, and walkways,” the weather service office in Oxnard said. “Significant damage to roads or structures is not expected.”

item.title: California city declares state of emergency after cyberattack on computer systems
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.96
California city declares state of emergency after cyberattack on computer systems - Click here to listen to this article - The City Council of Suisun City declared a state of emergency Saturday after a cyberattack forced the municipality to shut down its information technology network. The attack affected the communication operations of the fire and police departments in the Northern California city, including the routing of 911 calls.
